#47751. The future of tech will not be inclusive by default

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1175 w)

The future of tech will not be inclusive by default

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1175 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ten years ago, QueerTech began with a feeling that too many 2SLGBTQI+ people in the technology sector know well: not belonging.
  • My co-founder Andy Saldaña and I were working at different companies in tech and kept running into the same frustration.
  • Recent findings suggest that I grew up in Morocco, where being queer was, and continues to be, illegal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ten years ago, QueerTech began with a feeling that too many 2SLGBTQI+ people in the technology sector know well: not belonging.

My co-founder Andy Saldaña and I were working at different companies in tech and kept running into the same frustration. We could see the possibility of the sector around us, had the skills to succeed, and believed technology, when stewarded responsibly, could change lives. Yet we could not see a place for ourselves, as queer professionals, within it.

Recent findings suggest that I grew up in Morocco, where being queer was, and continues to be, illegal. In 2007, I left for Fresh York City in pursuit of the "American Dream." There, I promptly realized this dream was based on a contradiction — opportunity without equal rights. Finally, I moved to Montreal, drawn to Canada’s reputation for respecting people across cultures, religions, and identities.

Recent findings suggest that across this journey, I expected geography to change my sense of belonging. It never did. So in 2016, Andy and I started small. QueerTech was a volunteer-run community group built around a simple need: to find one another, create connections, and make space for queer people in an industry where many of us felt invisible.

Today, QueerTech is a national nonprofit working across workforce development, entrepreneurship, research, responsible technology, and community. Our scale has changed, but the need has not. What has evolved is our understanding of what meaningful inclusion requires: not only creating spaces where queer people belong, but breaking down the systemic barriers that determine who gets access to opportunities, who advances into leadership, and who has the power to shape the future of technology.

Recent findings suggest that the scope of our mission, spanning inclusive technology and professional wellbeing, demands ambitious goals and innovative programming grounded in collaboration and practical impact. Our community-first approach supports 2SLGBTQI+ professionals from industry entry through career advancement and entrepreneurship, while driving systemic change through partnerships with industry, investors, regulators, and community organizations.

QueerTech’s goals for the Canadian tech ecosystem are:.

Increasing 2SLGBTQI+ representation to 20 percent across the sector.

Advancing 2SLGBTQI+ leadership representation to 5 percent.

Increasing funding for 2SLGBTQI+-owned ventures to 15 percent of total invested capital.

QT Access: Building pathways into tech through skills development, mentorship and career preparation.

QT Leaders: Advancing professionals into decision-making roles that shape workplace culture, policy and innovation.

QT Founders: Equipping queer entrepreneurs with tools, networks and access to capital.

QT Events: Creating safer spaces for connection, learning and opportunity, both in-person and online.

Our responsible technology priorities center on the QT Inclusive AI Initiative. Launched in 2026, it combines self-assessment tools, inclusive AI training, national research, community dialogue, practical governance frameworks and cross-sector partnerships to strengthen AI literacy, accountability, inclusive practices, and collaboration.

According to recent reports, these efforts are grounded in a growing body of evidence about the barriers 2SLGBTQI+ professionals face, both within the technology sector and through the systems it creates. QueerTech’s 2026 research makes the scale of those challenges difficult to ignore.

It has been revealed that queerTech’s national Industry Census found 2SLGBTQI+ tech workers reported harassment and discrimination at roughly twice the rate of their non-2SLGBTQI+ peers: 44 percent reported harassment and 50 percent discrimination. Another 35 percent reported bias from AI hiring tools (versus 22 percent of peers). It has been revealed that inclusion in technology can no longer be measured only by who works inside the industry. We must also examine the systems the industry builds and deploys, including who participates in decisions, whose perspectives influence innovation, and who benefits from these advanced technologies.

This year, QueerTech studied both sides of that equation. Our research into AI development found 43 percent of Canadian technology companies reported limited to no formal processes for addressing bias, while 71 percent reported limited to no organizational support for equitable representation.

Our research into AI use in human resources also exposed a significant disconnect between institutional perceptions and queer professionals’ experiences. While 86 percent of HR professionals believed 2SLGBTQI+ employees were "comfortable being out," our 2026 Census found only 37 percent of queer professionals were "out" at work to a great extent — a disparity of nearly 50 percent.

The cost of that disconnect is higher than any one workplace. When queer professionals are overlooked, stalled or pushed out, companies lose skill, experience, and perspective. When people most likely to encounter bias are missing from product decisions, preventable blind spots can become features of automated systems and travel farther, faster and with less visibility.

According to recent reports, that is not just an inclusion problem. It is a talent, product, and competitiveness problem for Canada’s innovation economy. As Canada invests in its technological future and digital sovereignty, we cannot afford to overlook talent, limit leadership access, or build technologies that fail to serve the people who depend on them.

The next question is what the sector does with that evidence.

Sources indicate that on Nov. 18 and 19, more than 700 tech professionals will gather in Toronto for the 2026 QT Qonference (QTQ) under the theme Who Gets to Trust AI? This question is critical, given that trust in technology is shaped by various decentralized, and often competing, entities across the entire ecosystem. Developers build the systems. Employers decide how they are used. Executives set priorities. Policymakers create the rules. Workers and communities experience the results.

Recent findings suggest that QTQ convenes these groups to address the same challenges from different perspectives. Better decisions happen when the people building, governing, and using technology are at the same table, but participation alone is not enough. Meaningful change requires institutions to translate conversation into action: removing barriers to opportunity, embedding accountability into technology development and deployment, and giving affected communities a meaningful role in shaping these technologies.

According to recent reports, the future of tech will not be inclusive by default. It will be shaped by who is included in the decisions that define it. The responsibility belongs to all of us — industry leaders, investors, policymakers, and communities — to ensure that innovation expands opportunity rather than reinforces existing inequalities. Inclusion is not a concession to innovation; it’s a condition for responsible, sustainable innovation.

This article represents the opinion of its writer.

QueerTech is a national nonprofit advancing 2SLGBTQI+ talent, entrepreneurship, and inclusive technology across Canada’s tech ecosystem. Through community-led programming, original research, strategic partnerships, and actionable inclusion tools, QueerTech builds pathways to opportunity for queer professionals, leaders, and entrepreneurs while working with ecosystem partners to address the institutional barriers that limit access, advancement, and participation. Guided by its Vision 2034, QueerTech is working toward a technology ecosystem where queer people don't just participate — they thrive, lead, and help shape the future of innovation.

The tightest survival scrap for years? Why it's not too early to worry

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Is it too early for the Premier League bottom three to worry?
  • Despite being only 10 games into the season, sitting in the relegation zone even at this early stage is more worrying than you might think.
  • But with how tight the Premier League table is, this could also be one of the fiercest relegation battles we have seen in a long time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Is it too early for the Premier League bottom three to worry?

Despite being only 10 games into the season, sitting in the relegation zone even at this early stage is more worrying than you might think.

But with how tight the Premier League table is, this could also be one of the fiercest relegation battles we have seen in a long time.

Two of the current bottom three, Crystal Palace and Manchester United, will resume their campaigns at the weekend with new managers after appointing Thomas Frank and Mauricio Pochettino respectively.

Sunderland, wedged between the pair in 19th, have not pressed the panic button and have kept faith with Regis le Bris.

But is it too early to worry? We look at what the stats tell us about relegation battles in the past and what we can learn for the months ahead.

Looking at every Premier League season since it changed to a 20-team league in 1995-96, the current bottom three have cause to be concerned.

In 19 of the previous 31 seasons (61%), only one of the bottom three sides after 10 games managed to avoid relegation.

For fairness and accuracy, the 'bottom three' are the three sides with the worst record after 10 games, not simply those in the relegation zone after matchweek 10, since in some seasons a team had played nine games by that point.

Industry observers note that only in 10 seasons (32%) have two or more of the bottom three stayed up - and that has not happened in any of the past eight campaigns. The last time more than one team avoided the drop was in 2017-18, when all three survived.

That has only happened twice, although only twice have all three sides been relegated.

Overall, of the 93 previous teams in the bottom three after 10 games, 41 survived and 52 were relegated - a survival rate of 44%.

It has been revealed that this is the third time that Palace have been bottom after 10 games. On both previous occasions, they did not just survive but thrived, finishing 11th.

They did so under Tony Pulis in 2013-14 and under Roy Hodgson in 2017-18. Both managers, like Frank, were appointed early in the season following poor starts under Ian Holloway and Frank de Boer respectively.

The 2013-14 season is the only previous time that Sunderland and Palace were the bottom two at this stage. The Black Cats also survived thanks to a great, late escape under Gus Poyet.

This is the first time United have been in the bottom three after 10 games of a Premier League season.

Given the size and resources of the club, it is unlikely they will go down, although the team in 18th place at this stage have been relegated in each of the past six seasons.

Fans of all three clubs will hope for a repeat of 2017-18, when not only Palace but the bottom three improved significantly to finish comfortably mid-table.

While history suggests only one of the bottom three will survive, there is also evidence to suggest that this might not be a standard Premier League season.

Industry observers note that palace have seven points, which is the most the bottom side after 10 games have had for 24 years. The bottom three all had eight points in 2002-03.

Recent findings suggest that sunderland's eight points is also the most that a side in 19th place have had for 16 years. Wolves had nine points in 2010-11 and survived in 17th.

In fact, only five points separate the bottom half of the Premier League, with Tottenham in 11th on 12 points and Palace bottom with seven â the smallest gap at this stage for 24 years.

The highest that a team in the bottom three after 10 games have finished the season is eighth - Bolton in 2003-04, Tottenham in 2008-09 and Everton in 2017-18 - which suggests it will be Conference League at best for Manchester United next season.

Then again, the table is so tight that only nine points separate Chelsea in fifth and Palace - the smallest gap at this stage for 16 years.

Given that fifth place has been enough to qualify for the Champions League in recent seasons, optimistic United fans may not be ruling it out just yet.

That means even sides who have started well could be involved in the relegation battle.

The most points a team have had after 10 games of a 38-game season and been relegated is 14 - Joe Royle's Manchester City in 2000-01.

The most recent team to start well but be relegated were Eddie Howe's Bournemouth in 2019-20, who were sitting pretty in ninth with 13 points at this stage but went down on the final day.

As mentioned, this season has both the 'best' bottom side in terms of points and the most compact bottom half of the table that we have seen at this stage since 2002-03.

In that season, West Ham were relegated on the final day with 42 points - the most a side have been relegated with in Premier League history.

Given the way this season is shaping up, 40 points might also not be enough to survive.

NASA’s Parker Solar Probe discovers a hidden pattern in the Sun’s chaotic magnetic fields

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (817 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, turbulence is all around us, from milk swirling into a cup of coffee to powerful storms churning through the atmosphere and oceans.
  • Unlike the air and water on Earth, much of the matter in space consists of electrically charged particles in a state (known as the plasma state).
  • Industry observers note that scientists have long struggled to explain how turbulence develops under these conditions and how energy is distributed among its constantly changing fluctuations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, turbulence is all around us, from milk swirling into a cup of coffee to powerful storms churning through the atmosphere and oceans. But turbulence also occurs throughout space, where it behaves in ways that scientists are still struggling to understand.

Unlike the air and water on Earth, much of the matter in space consists of electrically charged particles in a state (known as the plasma state). These particles interact strongly with magnetic and electric fields, creating turbulence that is fundamentally different from what we experience on Earth. Space plasma is also so thinly spread that particles rarely collide with one another, making its behavior even more unusual.

Industry observers note that scientists have long struggled to explain how turbulence develops under these conditions and how energy is distributed among its constantly changing fluctuations. Now, an international research team has uncovered a surprising clue: hidden within the seemingly random motion of space plasma is a distinct magnetic pattern that reverses direction at very small scales.

The discovery, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, reveals a previously unobserved phenomenon that could improve our understanding of the solar wind and the turbulent conditions that influence space weather.

NASA's Parker Solar Probe Reveals a Hidden Magnetic Reversal.

Researchers from the Technische Universität Braunschweig and the University of Tokyo, working with Tohoku University, Kyushu University, Osaka University, and other international institutions, identified the phenomenon using observations from NASA's Parker Solar Probe.

The collaboration brought together scientists from ten countries, including researchers at the Institute of Theoretical Physics at Technische Universität Braunschweig.

In a recent development, by analyzing highly precise measurements of magnetic fields and particles, the team discovered that turbulent magnetic fields reverse their direction of rotation at a particular range of wavelengths. This marks the first direct observation of such a reversal in space turbulence.

Even more surprisingly, the reversal becomes more pronounced and shifts toward longer wavelengths as the solar wind travels farther from the Sun.

The change occurs at a critical boundary where the behavior of plasma shifts from the collective movement of a flowing fluid to the dynamics of individual particles. This connection suggests that the magnetic reversal may provide an crucial fresh way to understand how turbulence operates across different physical scales.

Finding Order in the Chaos of Space Turbulence.

At larger scales, plasma moves much like a fluid. Swirling structures called vortices and electromagnetic waves create increasingly complex fluctuations, producing the turbulent conditions found throughout space.

Although these movements appear random, the researchers discovered that the rotation of the magnetic fields follows a consistent pattern.

Sources indicate that when viewed along a direction pointing outward from the Sun, magnetic fields at larger scales tend to rotate counterclockwise. At much smaller scales, however, the preferred rotation switches to clockwise.

This reversal occurs precisely where plasma stops behaving primarily like a fluid and begins exhibiting behavior governed by individual particles.

The finding is particularly striking because it reveals a clear, organized feature within a system otherwise dominated by seemingly unpredictable fluctuations.

Sources indicate that "We see a clear structure in the spectrum, even though the turbulence represents unstructured motions," claims Dr. Masatomi Iizawa (TU Braunschweig), the study's first author.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Yokoi (University. of Tokyo) emphasizes the broader importance of the discovery, stating, "The results are of great significance for both plasma physics and astrophysics.".

Why the Discovery Matters for Solar Storms and Space Weather.

Although the magnetic reversal occurs at extremely small scales, understanding it could have far-reaching consequences for space physics.

Plasma turbulence is a major feature of many environments throughout the universe, including Earth's magnetosphere, the solar wind, regions affected by solar eruptions, interplanetary space, and the disks of material surrounding astronomical objects known as accretion disks.

It also influences the shock waves and clouds of magnetic material that travel through interplanetary space following eruptions on the Sun.

These disturbances can play an crucial role in geomagnetic storms, making plasma turbulence a critical factor in efforts to predict space weather.

Industry observers note that by showing how an organized magnetic pattern emerges as turbulent plasma transitions from fluid behavior to particle behavior, the new research provides an key piece of a longstanding physics puzzle. The findings could ultimately help scientists better understand the complex processes that govern the solar wind and improve the physical models used to forecast geomagnetic storms.

Czechia braces for massive protest against public media reform looks

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1045 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hundreds of thousands of people are expected to rally in Prague this weekend to protest the Czech government's bid to ram a bill to reform public media funding through parliament in a surprise overnight session in October.
  • In a recent development, the right-populist coalition headed by Prime Minister Andrej Babis fast-tracked the first of three readings of the legislation, which culminated in a vote of approval at 4:36 a.m.
  • The bill has already provoked numerous demonstrations and strikes across the country, but Sunday's gathering in the capital's Letna park is likely to be by far the largest to date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hundreds of thousands of people are expected to rally in Prague this weekend to protest the Czech government's bid to ram a bill to reform public media funding through parliament in a surprise overnight session in October.

In a recent development, the right-populist coalition headed by Prime Minister Andrej Babis fast-tracked the first of three readings of the legislation, which culminated in a vote of approval at 4:36 a.m. on October 24.

The bill has already provoked numerous demonstrations and strikes across the country, but Sunday's gathering in the capital's Letna park is likely to be by far the largest to date.

Under the government's proposal, the license fee model that presently funds Czech Television (CT) and Czech Radio (CRo) would be scrapped, and the broadcasters would be funded directly from the state budget.

The three parties in the coalition — Babis's centrist ANO, the far-right SPD, and radical conservative Motorists, whose voter bases tend to be less affluent — insist that the license fee is an unfair tax.

Sources indicate that the parties argue that the fresh arrangement, which would see funding for CT and CRo cut by around 15% in the first year, would make the two more efficient. They also point out that several other European Union states have made similar changes.

Critics have angrily dismissed these justifications.

Opposition parties, civil society organizations and international watchdogs accuse the government of seeking to undermine the independence of the broadcasters, whose critical reporting has long irked ANO and the SPD in particular.

Analysts point out that while models in other EU states include guarantees of long-term financial stability and editorial independence, the Czech government proposal offers neither.

CT and CRo have warned that the reduced budget included in the bill will mean programming- and staff cuts.

When the first publication of the proposed bill was met with protests over the summer, Vaclav Stetka of the European Latest School of Digital Studies told DW that such "dramatic budget cuts represent an act of cultural vandalism.".

There has also been condemnation of the restriction of the parliamentary debate amid the fast-tracking of the bill.

"The confrontational approach, the attempts to limit parliamentary debate and the government's rhetoric towards journalists and critics have all contributed to the public backlash," Otto Eibl, political scientist at Masaryk University in Czechia's second city Brno, told DW.

The backlash was immediate. Crowds picketed parliament through the night as the government pushed through the first reading of the bill.

Since then, multiple rallies have taken place in cities and towns across the country. Many of these protests were led by students and joined by unions, Churches and representatives of educational and cultural institutions.

CT and CRo staff called a strike in early November, disrupting the country's TV and radio schedules.

Sunday's protest is set to up the ante.

It will take place two days before the anniversary of the start of the Velvet Revolution, which ultimately brought down communism in what was then Czechoslovakia in 1989.

The civil society group Million Moments for Democracy, which is organizing Sunday's rally, brought an estimated 300,000 onto the streets to protest during Babis's first term as prime minister in 2019 and more than 200,000 earlier this year.

The government's sudden bid to push through the proposal reflects impatience to deliver on a core pledge made ahead of the October 2025 election, as well as the longstanding ambition of the prime minister, who was stymied in his attempt to engineer control of CT's governing council during his first term in power in 2017–21.

Vaclav Stetka notes that repeated assaults on public media by Czech governments past and present reflect a particular political culture across Europe's post-communist states.

"The political elite has never accepted the independence of public media," he asserted.

In Czechia, however, the public broadcasters have earned special status as cornerstones of democracy.

That standing was forged in what became known as the "Czech TV crisis" of 2000–01, when an occupation of CT's studios by staff and mass protests forced the government of the day to back down on a bid to wrest control.

"The fight over the public service media has become a symbol of the defense of liberal democratic values and institutions," Eibl stated.

In a recent development, as anger has swelled, the government has sought to calm the situation. Babis has said that a upcoming proposal, which would see public media funding moved off budget and editorial independence guaranteed, would be drawn up and made available for a full and open debate.

However, critics remain unimpressed, noting a lack of any detail and the fact that other members of the government appear determined to remain on course.

Million Moments for Democracy has insisted the pressure must continue.

It has been revealed that "Words are worth nothing," the group said. "While people stand up for independent media, the government continues to act as if it owns the country.".

With little sign that the opposition will dissipate, the government faces a choice.

It has the parliamentary majority it needs to push the bill through and defeat any likely vetoes from the upper house Senate and President Petr Pavel.

Polls suggest political support for the government has been weakened and could diminish further if the protests expand to include growing frustrations over the cost of living and housing, as happened recently with student-led protests in France and other European countries.

"The real risk for the government is that the media issue becomes a lightning rod for broader dissatisfaction," noted Martin Vokalek of the Prague-based EUROPEUM Institute for European Policy.

The PM revealed that he will not attend the Velvet Revolution anniversary celebrations on November 17, which are hugely symbolic, in the hope that his absence might "calm the tense situation.".

However, there's little concern that the Czech protests could descend into violence.

Analysts note that the anger in Czechia remains tightly focused on the public media proposal and continues to be expressed in a similar way to the seismic events of the country's modern history.

"I would not expect French-style scenes," Vokalek told DW, noting that the same "large, peaceful and civic Czech protest culture," which gave the Velvet Revolution and 1993's Velvet Divorce from Slovakia their name, is still strong.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jax Taylor is navigating a scary period in his health.

The Vanderpump Rules alum shared he’s been diagnosed with cancer after a tumor was discovered on his kidney during treatment for kidney stones in July.

In a recent development, “This is something I’ve kept private for the past few months because it’s been one of the scariest times of my life,” Taylor wrote in a Nov. 19 Instagram post, which featured photos from his hospital bed and a video of him walking with the help of a walker. “What I thought was just a kidney stone turned into something I never imagined. My CT scan also showed a tumor on my left kidney. After many tests and appointments I found out it was cancer.”.

The 47-year-old—who starred on Bravo’s Vanderpump Rules for eight seasons and the first two seasons of The Valley—shared that the diagnosis was especially challenging given his father had died of cancer. As he put of hearing the word cancer, “It broke me.”.

“It put me in a really dark place,” he added. “The hardest part was the waiting. Knowing there was a tumor growing inside me while trying to go about my life like everything was fine.”.

Taylor confirmed that prior to posting, he’d undergone a five-hour surgery to remove the tumor. He noted that the tumor was larger than doctors had anticipated, however, and that they’re awaiting further pathology results.

The former reality star—who was previously married to VPR costar Brittany Cartwright, with whom he shares 5-year-old son Cruz—expressed his gratitude for his medical team at Cedars Sinai and for his girlfriend, publicist Lori Krebs, as he navigates this scary period.

According to recent reports, “I honestly don’t know how I would have gotten through everything without my amazing girlfriend by my side,” he wrote of Krebs, who was seen lying in a hospital chair in one of the photos in Taylor’s carousel. “She’s been my rock through all of this. She’s not just my partner, she’s my best friend and I feel so insanely lucky to have her in my life.”.

Taylor also reflected on how the last few months have affected the way he views his health and wellbeing.

According to recent reports, “If there’s one thing I hope people can take away from this, it’s never to take your health for granted,” he wrote. “I did for many years and I won’t ever do that again.”.

In fact, his surgery coincides with a personal milestone.

“Next week on November 28 will mark my 2 year sobriety anniversary and I’m so f--king proud,” Taylor added. “It’s crazy how things happen…if I hadn’t ended up in the hospital with that kidney stone, I probably wouldn’t have known this tumor was there until it was too late. I like to think my dad had a part in that.”.

It has been revealed that he added, “Life can really change in a second. I’ve been given a lot to think about these past few years and if there’s one thing I know for sure it’s that nothing else matters more than your health your kids and the people that show up for you when it matters the most.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The assistant referee had a 60-day recovery period after being operated on.

An Ecuadorian footballer has been banned for eight years for throwing a rock at an assistant referee, leaving him requiring surgery to his face.

Jhon Perlaza was playing for Club Ciudad de Yantzaza against Club Rio Aguarico FC in a third-tier match in October when the incident took place.

The stone struck assistant referee Lenin Giovanni Ojeda Nunez in the face in the 96th minute of the game, which was subsequently abandoned.

A video on social media shows Perlaza standing up in the team's dugout to throw the stone, with Nunez instantly falling to the floor and holding his face after the object hits him. He then receives medical attention.

"The assistant referee suffered serious injuries that required surgery and a 60-day recovery period," the Ecuadorian Football Federation (FEF) stated.

"The disciplinary committee found the player responsible for physical aggression against a match official and suspended him for eight years from all football-related activity, until 19 October, 2034.

"In addition, the FEF will ask Fifa to extend this sanction worldwide.".

The FEF also fined his club Yantzaza $2,000 (Â£1,521) and ordered them to pay Nunez's medical fees of $4,369 (Â£3,323).

In a statement released on 20 October, three days after the match, Yantzaza apologised to the refereeing team and the fans, and confirmed Perlaza had been sacked as a result of the incident.

Recent findings suggest that "As an institution, we categorically reject all acts of aggression, whether verbal or physical, both inside and outside sporting venues. We firmly believe that football should be a space of respect, coexistence, and fair play," they said.

"Once the person responsible for this regrettable incident was identified, the institution made the decision to remove him immediately, and he is therefore no longer part of our club.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tessa Brown is visibly excited to talk to me about Germ DM, her secure messaging platform.
  • “It's essential to be able to talk to everybody, and that's really what this Android launch unlocks for us,” she claims.
  • The platform expansion makes it easier to recommend Germ as an interesting alternative to Signal, especially for early adopters curious about trying upcoming ways to message others and connect with the world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tessa Brown is visibly excited to talk to me about Germ DM, her secure messaging platform. It’s now available on Android, a major expansion for the small startup. Her eyes light up as she explains how her ambitious, three-person team—including an ex-Apple engineer who worked on iMessage—could pull off this platform expansion.

“It's essential to be able to talk to everybody, and that's really what this Android launch unlocks for us,” she claims. Brown was previously a lecturer at Stanford University, and her cofounder, Mark Xue, worked on iMessage’s privacy provisions. The duo first debuted the iOS app for Germ in 2023.

The platform expansion makes it easier to recommend Germ as an interesting alternative to Signal, especially for early adopters curious about trying upcoming ways to message others and connect with the world.

Tessa Brown and Mark Xue, cofounders of Germ Network.

According to recent reports, the app revolves around “burner cards.” Each card works like a separate phone line built into the app. Instead of a dedicated number or a public handle, you can share these Germ cards in two ways: a QR code or a direct link. You can scan QR codes inside the app if meeting someone in person. For digital connections, you can generate a custom link tied to the card, from just one to 100.

In a recent development, after downloading the app, you create these cards by tapping on the green plus button under the Me tab. Choose the name, pronouns, and photo you want to use for that card. Cards associated with your Germ account are not mutually discoverable, and who you connect with on each card is private. As the name suggests, if you delete these “burners” at any time, the connections associated with that card will no longer be able to contact you, and those chats will be removed from your device.

The Germ network runs on Messaging Layer Security, built by the Internet Engineering Task Force as an end-to-end encryption standard. When you are exchanging those “burner cards,” you are actually exchanging cryptographic keys with your newly introduced contacts. However, Germ has not undergone a third-party audit, though Brown is open to doing so in the future.

Recent findings suggest that “People want to share different parts of themselves with different people,” Brown says. “Queer folks get Germ immediately; it's not just queer people. It's also people who are gig workers and creatives that have multiple jobs.” Germ is built to share with people in different parts of your life and let them contact you in a central hub through distinct messaging channels.

According to recent reports, xue is serious about the work Germ put into building a secure platform, including addressing the looming glitch of quantum computing. Essentially, security experts worry that super-powerful computers could break encryption protections and reveal previously private messages. Developers at large messaging platforms, like iMessage and Signal, have built protections against these quantum concerns. “What we've accomplished as a small team is we've reached the same level of security,” he claims. Germ publicly laid out how the platform claims to be “quantum secure.”.

Germ’s most recent success came from its integration with Bluesky. Since that social media platform is built on the Authenticated Transfer Protocol, Bluesky users can connect their existing handles to Germ and display it as a messaging button in their profile. This lets friends on the platform easily send you encrypted texts. While many users enjoy that platform-specific integration, Germ’s expansion to Android is a fresh opportunity to meet a upcoming user base.

Brown already has her sights set on Germ’s next move: group chats.

Industry observers note that “We’ve worked together this whole time over the belief that the future of communication is in private chats,” she indicates. For now, the platform supports one-on-one conversations, but the team is ready to build support for larger, group threads.

It might be hard to convince your group chat to switch to a new app, but flashing a QR code to a stranger you just met to continue a conversation could actually work.

The mystery of how hair knows where to grow may finally be solved

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (820 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Long before a mammal is born, its skin begins establishing the precise locations where hair will eventually grow.
  • Researchers at the University of Geneva (UNIGE) have identified a surprisingly simple process that may help explain this biological mystery.
  • The discovery could help explain a much broader phenomenon in nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Long before a mammal is born, its skin begins establishing the precise locations where hair will eventually grow. These developing hair follicles form intricate geometric arrangements that differ from species to species. But what determines where each follicle appears, and how does the body create such orderly patterns?

Researchers at the University of Geneva (UNIGE) have identified a surprisingly simple process that may help explain this biological mystery. By studying how cells move in response to chemical signals, the team developed a model that successfully recreates the formation of hair follicle patterns in two mammalian species. Their findings, published in PNAS, suggest that elaborate biological structures can emerge naturally from basic interactions between neighboring cells.

The discovery could help explain a much broader phenomenon in nature. Hair, feathers, and most types of scales begin as small structures called placodes that appear during embryonic development. Scientists have spent decades investigating how these early structures establish the distinctive arrangements seen across different animal species.

Challenging a Long-Standing Theory of Hair Growth.

In a recent development, for laboratory mice (Mus musculus), the leading explanation has traditionally been the expansion-induction model. This theory proposes that when a new placode appears, it releases a chemical that prevents additional placodes from developing too close to it.

As the embryo's skin grows and stretches, some areas move far enough away from existing placodes to escape the chemical's influence. Newly introduced placodes can then develop in those spaces, gradually creating a more complete pattern across the skin.

Although this explanation has gained widespread acceptance, scientists have not experimentally established that it can account for the diversity of follicle patterns found across species.

A Simpler Mechanism for Hair Follicle Formation.

To investigate another possibility, researchers led by Athanasia Tzika, Senior Lecturer, and Michel Milinkovitch, Professor, both in the Department of Genetics and Evolution at UNIGE's Faculty of Science, focused on a process called chemotaxis.

In a recent development, chemotaxis occurs when cells move in response to differences in chemical concentrations. The same basic process helps guide white blood cells toward areas of inflammation, allowing the immune system to respond where it is needed.

The researchers created a mathematical model that tracks how mobile cells in the dermis interact with an attracting chemical signal released by the epidermis, the skin's outer layer. They then simulated the growth of embryonic skin to see whether these interactions could produce the gradual appearance of placodes.

Remarkably, the model recreated the developmental patterns observed in laboratory mice, including the same sequence of follicle formation that scientists had previously explained using the expansion-induction theory. This suggests that a complex system of instructions may not be necessary to determine where follicles develop.

"Our findings show that the observed patterns do not require a complex system telling each placode where to form," explain Muhamet Ibrahimi and Ebrahim Jahanbakhsh, researchers in the Department of Genetics and Evolution. "Instead, placodes emerge spontaneously from local interactions between cells and chemical signals.".

One Simple Process Creates Different Hair Patterns.

The team next investigated whether the same mechanism could explain follicle arrangements in another mammal with a very different coat structure.

They selected the spiny mouse (Acomys dimidiatus), a rodent whose hair follicles develop in an unusually regular pattern with a strong directional alignment. This distinctive organization cannot be explained by the traditional expansion-induction model.

Using experimental information gathered from three-dimensional images of developing embryonic skin, the researchers adapted their simulations to reflect the spiny mouse's particular biochemical characteristics and the way its skin grows.

Industry observers note that the results showed that the same underlying process of cells responding to chemical signals could also reproduce the spiny mouse's highly organized follicle pattern. The differences between the two species could be explained by variations in their cellular interactions, chemical properties, and skin growth rather than entirely different mechanisms.

It has been revealed that these findings suggest that the remarkable variety of structures found throughout the animal kingdom may arise from a shared set of relatively simple biological rules. By adjusting how cells interact and respond to their surroundings, nature can generate dramatically different patterns without requiring a separate developmental blueprint for every species.

"Our work suggests that simple cellular interactions can generate the remarkable diversity of tissue architectures observed throughout evolution," concludes Athanasia Tzika. "The differences observed between species therefore result from the same self-organization process, but with variations in the interactions between cells and chemical signals.".

Industry News: What exactly is a light-day? Here's what Voyager 1's latest milestone means for the interstellar probe

💡 Key Takeaways
  • After nearly 50 years traveling through space, NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is approaching a milestone no human-made object has reached before: a distance of one light-day from Earth.
  • Industry observers note that this milestone — which Voyager 1 is expected to reach on Wednesday, Nov.
  • Astronomers use a measurement known as a light-day to describe how far light travels in 24 hours.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After nearly 50 years traveling through space, NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is approaching a milestone no human-made object has reached before: a distance of one light-day from Earth.

Industry observers note that this milestone — which Voyager 1 is expected to reach on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, at 5:16:07 a.m. EST (1016:07 GMT) — highlights the immense distances Voyager 1 has traveled and the challenges of communicating with spacecraft operating in the outer reaches of the solar system and beyond.

Astronomers use a measurement known as a light-day to describe how far light travels in 24 hours. Light moves at approximately 186,000 miles (300,000 kilometers) per second, meaning one light-day is roughly 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), according to a statement from NASA.

Although the term light-day might sound like a measurement of time, it is actually a unit of distance, much like a light-year. Astronomers use light-based measurements because conventional miles and kilometers become increasingly difficult to comprehend when describing the enormous distances between objects in space.

Sources indicate that for perspective on how far Voyager 1 has travelled, sunlight takes about eight minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth, meaning our planet is approximately 8.3 light-minutes from the sun. Radio signals traveling between Earth and Mars can take anywhere from three to 22 minutes, depending on the planets' positions in their orbits, according to the statement.

By comparison, when Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth, a radio signal sent from the probe will take a full 24 hours to reach mission controllers on Earth, and a command transmitted from Earth will take another 24 hours to reach the spacecraft.

The communication delay affects how engineers operate spacecraft at such distances. Unlike spacecraft operating closer to Earth, which can receive commands and return data with relatively little delay, communicating with Voyager 1 requires mission controllers to account for the extended signal travel time when planning spacecraft operations, troubleshooting technical challenges and evaluating the results of commands sent to the probe.

It has been revealed that voyager 1 has been traveling away from Earth since its launch on Sept. 5, 1977. Now cruising through interstellar space at nearly 38,000 mph (61,000 kph), the spacecraft has spent more than 49 years covering the distance that light can cross in a single day.

It has been revealed that even at that speed, Voyager 1 is moving relatively slowly compared with light itself. Its twin, Voyager 2, which debuted in 1977 on a different trajectory, is expected to reach the same one-light-day milestone in November 2035.

As Voyager 1 and, eventually, Voyager 2 continue their journeys through interstellar space, their growing distances from Earth offer a measure of both the reach of human exploration and the communication challenges that come with sending spacecraft ever farther into the cosmos.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • German Chancellor Friedrich Merz got a birthday cake at the UN climate summit in Turkey this week.
  • Sources indicate that fridays for Future is taking its demands to German streets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These updates have been closed. Below, you can review our collection of news and analysis on stories from or relating to Germany from Friday, November 13.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz got a birthday cake at the UN climate summit in Turkey this week. But he wasn't there to eat it. Meanwhile, in Berlin, climate activists marked his 71st birthday on Friday with a symbolic chocolate cake. Their message: they too want to reach that age on a livable planet.

Sources indicate that fridays for Future is taking its demands to German streets. Demonstrations were planned in more than 70 German cities on Friday, November 13.

Under the slogan "Pay your climate debt," protesters in the German capital demanded more funding for climate protection and adaptation in developing countries, alongside a global phase-out of coal, oil and gas.

Germany provided €4.7 billion ($5.2 billion) in federal budget funds for international climate financing in 2025 — below its €6 billion pledge.

But the protest movement is no longer drawing the crowds it once did. In September 2019, Fridays for Future mobilized an estimated 1.4 million people across Germany. Five years later, that figure fell to around 75,000 at a comparable nationwide strike.

According to recent reports, this comes as broader youth frustration with German politics grows. "I don't feel addressed by the chancellor unfortunately," Kim, a protester in Berlin, told DW.

From military service to affordable housing and climate policy, younger Germans are questioning whether their concerns are being heard.

In a recent development, A recent nationwide poll found that 82% of Germans believe politicians do not adequately represent young people's interests. Among 18- to 34-year-olds, just 5% trust Merz's conservatives to champion their concerns, compared with 3% for their Social Democratic coalition partners.

Recent findings suggest that merz is not the first German chancellor to miss a UN climate summit. And smaller demonstrations do not necessarily mean young Germans care less about climate change. But the contrast is striking: while the climate movement struggles to mobilize, dissatisfaction among younger voters extends well beyond environmental policy.

Julian Reichelt, formerly the editor-in-chief of Germany's top-selling tabloid Bild, says he was the target of an arson attack after his car was set on fire and largely destroyed in Berlin.

Now editor-in-chief of the right-wing online portal Nius that he co-founded, Reichelt stated the arson attack took place in the Charlottenburg district of the German capital overnight.

It has been revealed that police confirmed the car was intentionally set alight, saying a passerby reported it shortly after 2 a.m. that morning. However, they did not name a suspect or potential personal motive at first, saying only that the fire department responded and extinguished the fire.

"It is completely clear that this was a targeted attack," Reichelt said, calling it an "attempt at intimidation against upcoming free media that stand up against this left-wing extremism.".

Similar arson attacks several years ago targeted cars belonging to a columnist for another Berlin newspaper, B.Z., with a left-wing group claiming responsibility in one case.

Recent findings suggest that that said, Berlin also has a more general and fairly well documented problem with arson and vandalism targeting cars, with an average of roughly two a night being set alight in the capital city over recent years. Vandalism and insurance fraud are the most common reasons more generally.

Reichelt was fired from his prominent job at Bild in 2021 amid allegations of sexual harassment, accusations he always denied and referred to as a "smear campaign.".

Lawmakers in the Bundestag have approved reforms that will provide additional powers to Germany's domestic and external intelligence agencies.

The changes will strengthen both the external Federal Intelligence Service (BND) and domestic intelligence service the BfV, formally titled the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution.

The law passed fairly comfortably in the federal Bundestag lower house of parliament, with 309 votes in favor, 190 against and 71 abstentions.

The BfV will be granted powers beyond intelligence gathering and monitoring individuals, such as being able to secretly enter homes or take action against explosives or weapons.

In the case of the BND, it will be granted additional operational intervention powers, for instance moving to disable servers belonging to state-sponsored hacker groups abroad.

The changes aim to respond to intensified and evolving threats from foreign intelligence services and their partners, and to reduce dependency on information supplied by friendly foreign intelligence services.

Opposition parties have accused the government of abolishing or weakening the separation between the police and intelligence services — a sensitive and closely monitored distinction in German society, because of the legacy both of Adolf Hitler's Nazi regime and of the secret police services in Communist East Germany during the Cold War.

Friedrich Merz has remarked during his visit to Dublin that Germany and Europe's position in future peace talks for Ukraine is "set.".

Following the talks in Abu Dhabi this week between Ukraine and Russia brokered by the US, which also involved European representatives at times, Merz said further negotiations were now planned.

"In the coming weeks there should now be concrete peace talks in which Europe is represented," Merz told reporters in Dublin amid an informal meeting of EU leaders.

He mentioned that "provisionally" this might involve the same "group of Europeans" who had participated in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday.

"Germany is set in there, that is completely clear," he remarked.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz's call to link EU budget negotiations to the provision of assistance to Ukraine, which faced hefty criticism at home, has found some backing amid European Political Community meetings and an AI summit in Dublin.

Merz, who has been leading the charge to find savings in the next EU budget, said doing so could ensure stronger contributions to helping Ukraine from all EU member states.

Estonia's Prime Minister Kristen Michal noted during the meeting in Dublin that he approved of Merz's suggestion "that support for Ukraine is also a part of our core security and our core financing.".

He noted that members who wanted a newly introduced EU budget should contribute.

Latvia's Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, meanwhile, said he agreed completely with Merz.

"We must all pull in the same direction. All of Europe must do its part," he noted.

Luxembourg's Luc Frieden also said that "we must all stand behind Ukraine" and added that collective financial commitments should be a part of this.

As the largest economy and most populous country in the EU, Germany is the largest overall contributor both to the EU budget and to assistance for Ukraine.

Countries that tend to be so-called net beneficiaries of the EU budget, rather than net contributors to it, tend to be more reticent to cut spending plans.

Hosts Ireland, in a tricky position as the holders of the rotating presidency of the EU trying to broker a deal on the next seven-year budget, remarked it had concerns about adding an additional factor to the stalled talks, as the current budget's expiry at the end of 2027 starts to draw near.

Sources indicate that "But I do understand why this is happening," Taoiseach (or prime minister) Micheal Martin mentioned in Dublin. "Some countries have made considerable contributions and they want all EU member states to contribute financially to the support for Ukraine.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) was critical of both the spending and the fundraising prepares in the 2027 budget, claiming without showing its workings that it would be able to do more with less by making swingeing cuts in various key areas.

Budget policy spokesman Michael Espendiller mentioned the budget meant "more debts and more taxes and more burdens for the taxpayer.".

In a recent development, he accused the Christian Democrats of breaking key election pledges by raising taxes on alcohol and tobacco. He then complained that despite this, there was not enough money for the promised electricity tax cut.

"If you put it into figures, the federal government will be taking out almost €400,000 (around $440,000) every minute in upcoming debt," Espendiller said, calling for an end to what he called a spiral of debt.

He claimed that the AfD would have able to complete its budget with newly introduced debt of just €63 billion, not roughly €210 billion, while simultaneously providing tax relief of around €44 billion.

Espendiller said this would be achieved with wide-reaching cuts in several core areas of spending: climate protection, contributing to the EU budget and other EU funding, asylum-related spending, international development aid, and weapons deliveries and other assistance to Ukraine.

It's unclear to what extent these proposed cuts would be feasible or legal, or what domestic or international implications they might have, or whether they'd save anything like the amount the AfD asserts in practice.

Politicians on the Bundestag budget committee burned the proverbial candle at both ends heading into Friday morning, trying to finalize details of the federal government's spending prepares for 2027 before the year's end.

The session took over 15 hours, and already politicians are talking about areas where they still see room for further improvement or alteration — but the document does at least stand in such a form in which it can take effect without too many complications.

Including all spending intends, in the core budget and from the so-called "special funds" for infrastructure and military modernization, fresh debt constitutes around a third of oultays.

In total, the strategy is to take out latest debt worth just over €210 billion ($233 billion), while taking in a little less than €400 billion in taxes.

According to recent reports, that's the second-highest level of newly introduced debt in the post-war history of the Federal Republic of Germany. Even at the height of the COVID pandemic in 2021, new debt was only slightly higher, at €215.4 billion.

We'll likely be returning to the various details of and reactions to this story throughout the morning.

The environmentalist Greens took aim at Chancellor Merz for not delivering on a promise to reduce taxes on electricity in the final budget.

"The big promise that Chancellor Merz made a few days ago, sinking electricity taxes for everyone, this promise remains a broken promise," party co-leader Britta Hasselmann mentioned on ZDF television on Friday.

"It was possible to find a way at short notice for several other things in this budget," she said.

"I think this demonstrates the inadequate planning and the weak leadership of the chancellor," Hasselmann stated.

She added that the CDU forcing a delay to the planned sugar tax at short notice was further evidence of the planning shortcomings.

A budget expert at the party, Sebastian Schäfer, similarly alleged a "leadership vacuum in this coalition government," saying that what was put forward was less a budget and more a "wooden shack wihtout foundations.".

The Left Party's budget policy spokesman Dietmar Bartsch has lamented a "knot garden of debt, tricks and delays," accusing the coalition of not conducting "responsible budgetary policy.".

Despite criticizing the debt levels, Bartsch also noted it was "deeply unserious" to float electricity tax relief but then withdraw the plan.

It has been revealed that he mentioned this would have cost less money than the federal government's strategy to buy a share of the arms company KNDS. He also said it was unacceptable for the center-left Social Democrats to be celebrating just because "the odd welfare cut is not happening.".

Ines Schwerdtner, co-leader of the party that firmly opposes defense spending and is at best lukewarm on NATO membership, noted the record spending demonstrated that money was not as tight as Merz's government made out.

"The debt brake is suspended for weapons, but for housing and electricity taxes they scrimp for every euro," Schwerdtner said. "The money is there, this government is just distributing it completely incorrectly.".

Schwerdtner, herself a member of the budget committed in the Bundestag, called it a "budget of naivete.".

More on this morning's top story in Berlin, the 2027 budget being signed off.

As the CDU calls for further savings, the Social Democrats say that the energy tax relief recently touted by Chancellor Friedrich Merz "would have to be financed with additional debts.".

Ahead of Thursday's marathon talks, Merz had said he hoped to introduce the tax relief amid the stress caused by concerns including the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

The SPD's Dirk Wiese said the junior coalition partners were "not disinclined to pave the way for the electricity tax relief," but not by making cuts elsewhere.

Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil of the SPD had stated he did not see enough fiscal wiggle room to enable the desired tax break.

Bremen's mayor Andreas Bovenshulte, also a Social Democrat, said that while he would have welcomed the relief, other decisions meant it wasn't possible.

"For that, a serious financing source would have been required, for instance with a plastic or sugar of windfall tax," Bovenschulte noted, in reference to either delayed or proposed but rejected looks to potentially increase tax revenues.

German defense industry startup Quantum Systems said its drones were operational worldwide once again, including with the Bundeswehr military, after a cyberattack by "hostile actors" last month.

The company had declared the cyberattack on Thursday, amid reporting from the Financial Times that also said the Bundeswehr had grounded its drones from the company.

Industry observers note that "The fleet is operating normally around the globe — including Germany and the Bundeswehr," a Quantum Systems spokesperson said in an emailed statement to the Reuters news agency. "The Bundeswehr was the only customer to ground their systems as a precaution.".

The company, based near Munich, had earlier mentioned it uncovered an "active cyberattack" by hostile actors.

"The threat was contained thanks to the swift response of our IT and security teams in close and transparent collaboration with the authorities," it stated in a statement, adding there was no risk for end customers and operators using its unmanned systems.

Quantum drones are used by Ukrainian armed forces in their defensive war against Russia, among others.

"Companies at the forefront of supporting Ukraine are being targeted precisely because our work is critically relevant to customers' security," the tech giant said. "Being aware of this responsibility, Quantum Systems has mitigation plans in place and strives to fulfil the highest standard of data and system security.".

Senior Christian Democrat Union (CDU) politician Matthias Middelberg appeared on ZDF television this morning to discuss the budget breakthrough.

He identified one "weak point" after the overnight negotiations.

"We have not yet saved enough, we still need to save a lot more," he stated.

Middelberg said that in his view the government would not be able to "collect the funds," because that would put too much tax strain on people and businesses.

Therefore, he said, "the government must make cutbacks.".

Middelberg acepted that it wasn't clear how to do this, speculating that "perhaps there are subsidies or some other things" that could be ripe to be trimmed.

He mentioned the leadership of the coalition government's CDU/CSU and Social Democrats would "consider this question very closely once more.".

The German government statistics agency Destatis has published upcoming figures on insolvency filings for the month of August.

A total of 2,067 companies registered insolvencies with German courts during the month, Destatis noted, 4.4% more than in the same month in 2025.

The data operates on something of a delay, because the government tracks when courts grant the status, which can be almost three months after the initial application at times.

The increase has been a rolling trend this year. From January to August, 17,252 companies have filed for insolvency, 6.6% more than in the same period last year.

However, the total sum of debts forgiven in insolvency proceedings is actually quite considerably lower than in the first eight months of last year, at €25.9 billion ($28.7 billion) rather than €37.2 billion, because fewer large companies have gone bust.

In a recent development, more individuals are also filing for bankruptcy protection than in 2025, although the rise is somewhat less sharp. In August, 6,301 people gained insolvency protection, 2.8% more than last August. For January through August, the year-on-year increase is more modest, at 1.2%.

The proverbial white smoke emerged at around 6 in the morning in Berlin, with word of a finalized agreement.

If you were tired of talk and criticism of the "debt brake" and the "black zero" (a promise not to take any newly introduced debts) in the years following the eurozone debt crisis, rest assured we can assign such chatter to the history books for now.

The borrowing looks for 2027 — if you incorporate new debt taken out as part of so-called "special funds," for instance for the military and infrastructure, rather than as part of the core budget — are the second highest in the history of post-war Germany.

#47735. Breaking: Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low

Breaking: Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1618 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have uncovered fresh clues about why some people develop heart disease even after lowering their bad cholesterol to recommended levels.
  • Heart disease remains one of the world's leading causes of death.
  • According to recent reports, reducing LDL cholesterol, commonly known as "bad cholesterol," is a proven way to lower the likelihood of a heart attack.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have uncovered fresh clues about why some people develop heart disease even after lowering their bad cholesterol to recommended levels. Their findings point to biological processes involving other fat-carrying particles in the blood that may contribute to cardiovascular damage in ways that go beyond cholesterol buildup. By identifying these previously poorly understood mechanisms, the research could help pave the way for more targeted strategies to prevent heart disease and potentially save lives.

Heart disease remains one of the world's leading causes of death. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), cardiovascular diseases kill nearly 17.9 million people worldwide each year, with heart attacks and strokes responsible for more than 80% of those deaths. Coronary heart disease develops when fatty deposits containing cholesterol (cholesterol) build up inside the arteries that supply blood to the heart. If left untreated, the condition can eventually cause a heart attack.

According to recent reports, reducing LDL cholesterol, commonly known as "bad cholesterol," is a proven way to lower the likelihood of a heart attack. However, bringing LDL cholesterol into the recommended range does not eliminate the danger. Some patients continue to develop coronary heart disease despite successful treatment, suggesting that other particles transporting fats through the bloodstream play an crucial role. Until recently, the biological reasons behind this remaining risk were not well understood.

"For this study, we wanted to understand what happens beyond the accumulation of cholesterol in artery walls, whether different fat-carrying particles can damage the blood vessels differently and why the remaining risk of heart disease still occurs," says Jakub Morze, lead author and a postdoctoral fellow at Chalmers University of Technology, in Sweden.

According to recent reports, cholesterol is a substance similar to fat that circulates in the bloodstream. The body needs it to build cells and manufacture certain vitamins and hormones. Problems can arise when too much cholesterol accumulates in blood vessel walls, creating deposits called plaques.

It has been revealed that these plaques can narrow arteries and interfere with blood flow. If a plaque ruptures, a blood clot may form swiftly and completely obstruct the affected vessel, potentially triggering a heart attack or stroke.

Sources indicate that because cholesterol and other fats cannot travel through the blood on their own, they are transported by specialized particles known as lipoproteins. Three major classes of these particles contain a surface protein called apolipoprotein B (apoB). When too many of these particles circulate in the blood, they can deliver excess cholesterol into artery walls. The cholesterol they carry is commonly referred to as "bad cholesterol.".

To investigate these unanswered questions, the scientists used proteomics analysis to examine how three types of fat-carrying particles (LDL, TRL and Lp(a)) affect the body and may contribute to heart disease. This approach allowed the team to investigate biological changes associated with the particles rather than focusing exclusively on the cholesterol they carry.

According to recent reports, all three types can contribute to cholesterol deposits inside artery walls, although LDL, which stands for low-density lipoprotein, is the most common. In a previous study, the same research group found that counting harmful lipoprotein particles was the most effective way to predict future heart disease risk.

In a recent development, the researchers also identified two particularly important contributors beyond LDL: triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, or TRL, and lipoprotein(a), known as Lp(a). Their earlier findings suggested that each of these particles poses a greater risk individually than an LDL particle. As a result, TRL and Lp(a) are considered major contributors to the cardiovascular danger that can persist even after LDL cholesterol has been successfully reduced.

Proteomics is the systematic, large-scale examination and measurement of proteins within cells, tissues, or body fluids at a particular point in time.

While genomics investigates a person's relatively stable DNA, proteomics focuses on proteins, which are constantly responding to changes inside the body. These molecules help construct tissues, process food, transmit hormonal messages, and defend against infections.

Recent findings suggest that because protein patterns shift in response to factors such as diet, stress, aging, and disease, analyzing them can provide a snapshot of current biological activity. Proteomics can help researchers identify biomarkers, diagnose medical conditions, and track how patients respond to treatment.

Blood Proteins Reveal Hidden Heart Disease Risks.

In a recent development, the new investigation focused on proteins, which perform countless essential functions throughout the body. Unlike genetic information, which remains largely unchanged, protein levels and activity can respond to diet, stress, aging, and illness. Studying these changes can therefore provide valuable insights into the body's current biological condition.

Researchers analyzed measurements of nearly 3,000 proteins found in blood samples and compared the results with genetic information and long-term health records. This combination helped them identify protein patterns associated with different lipoprotein particles and provided clues about how those particles might contribute to damage inside the arteries.

One of the most striking discoveries involved TRL and Lp(a). Although these are distinct types of particles, their associated blood protein patterns demonstrated substantial similarities. Those overlapping patterns also appeared to be linked to the later development of heart disease.

According to recent reports, the researchers found that these particles carried proteins capable of attracting immune cells, potentially encouraging inflammation and changes in the structure of blood vessel walls. This suggests that TRL and Lp(a) may contribute to cardiovascular disease through some of the same biological processes, rather than simply depositing cholesterol in the arteries.

In a recent development, LDL showed a different pattern. Its associated proteins were primarily connected to cholesterol accumulation in artery walls, highlighting an important distinction between the ways these three types of particles may contribute to heart disease.

"The overlap for TRL and Lp(a) is one of the most interesting findings," says Morze. "It suggests that these particles may affect some of the same inflammatory and vascular processes. This could help identify targets for more precisely directed prevention in the future.".

How LDL, TRL, and Lp(a) Affect Heart Health.

According to recent reports, the three types of lipoproteins examined in the study, LDL, TRL, and Lp(a), transport different amounts of cholesterol and other fats through the bloodstream. Each contains the structural protein apolipoprotein B, or apoB.

Sources indicate that all three can contribute to atherosclerosis, a condition in which fatty material accumulates inside blood vessel walls. As these deposits develop, they increase the risk of coronary heart disease.

LDL: Low-density lipoprotein transports most of the cholesterol circulating in the blood. An LDL cholesterol measurement indicates how much cholesterol is contained within these particles.

TRL: Triglyceride-rich lipoproteins transport cholesterol along with triglycerides, which the body uses as an vital energy source. As triglycerides are removed from these particles, the remaining fragments can deposit cholesterol inside artery walls. In this study, the TRL measurements primarily reflected liver-produced particles called VLDL and the remnants they leave behind.

Industry observers note that lp(a): Lipoprotein(a) resembles an LDL particle but contains an additional protein known as apolipoprotein(a). Higher levels of Lp(a) are already recognized as an established risk factor for coronary heart disease.

Could the Discovery Lead to Better Heart Disease Prevention?

It has been revealed that by identifying biological pathways associated with cardiovascular risk beyond LDL cholesterol, the findings offer researchers new possibilities for developing more personalized prevention strategies. In particular, the shared inflammatory and blood vessel effects linked to TRL and Lp(a) could become promising areas for further investigation.

However, the research did not evaluate a upcoming treatment or establish a blood protein test ready for routine clinical use. Additional studies will be needed to determine whether measuring these biological processes, or developing treatments that target them, can improve protection against heart disease.

"Lowering LDL cholesterol remains a cornerstone of prevention," indicates Clemens Wittenbecher, who led the study and is Assistant Professor of Precision Medicine and Diagnostics at Chalmers. "Our findings point to biological processes that may help explain some of the risk that remains beyond LDL. The next step is to establish whether measuring or targeting these processes can improve prevention alongside existing treatments.".

Recent findings suggest that the results reinforce the importance of controlling LDL cholesterol while revealing why cholesterol reduction alone may not address every source of cardiovascular risk. Understanding the additional ways blood particles affect arteries could ultimately help scientists develop more precise approaches to protecting heart health.

Study Details and Research Institutions.

The study, "Apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins: distinct roles in atherosclerosis revealed by plasma proteomic profiling," was published in the European Heart Journal.

The research authors are Jakub Morze, Elias Björnson, Michael Y Mi, Martin Adiels, Giorgio E Melloni, Gonçalo Rosas da Silva, Andrzej Rynkiewicz, Nicholas A Marston, Marta Guasch-Ferré, Michael Y Tsai, Jerome I Rotter, Robert E Gerszten, Qi Sun, Frank B Hu, Rikard Landberg, Göran Bergström, Chris J Packard, Jan Borén and Clemens Wittenbecher.

According to recent reports, at the time of the research, the authors were affiliated with Chalmers University of Technology and the Institute of Medicine at the University of Gothenburg, Sweden; Harvard Medical School, USA; AstraZeneca, Sweden; Municipal Hospital in Olsztyn, Poland; University of Copenhagen, Denmark; University of Minnesota, USA; The Lundquist Institute at Harbour-UCLA Medical Center in Torrance, USA; Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health in Boston, USA; and the University of Glasgow, UK.

Materials provided by Chalmers University of Technology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Wales in fight to retain rising female stars.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It looks like Taylor Swift still has plenty of tricks up her sleeve—or rather snakes in her boot?

As the “I Knew It, I Knew You” singer took the stage at the CMA Awards Nov. 18 to perform a medley of her newest country hit as well as one of her first, “Our Song,” many fans noticed there may be several Easter eggs hinting at the re-release of her debut album.

The first clue fans noticed was dropped before Swift even started singing, as she began her performance in a backstage dressing room that was decorated with several familiar pieces of clothing, namely dresses she wore during her first rodeo.

In a recent development, for one, there was the butter yellow ballgown she wore to the CMA Awards in 2007—the year she scored her very first win—that was strewn across the couch behind Swift. Then, hanging on a clothing rack to her right, was a floral print halter dress that Swift wore to the Academy of Country Music Awards in 2006, which was one of the very first major red carpet walks of her career.

Industry observers note that even more noteworthy were the final two dresses fans noticed. One purple-looking dress that was directly behind Swift on a couch, mostly obscured from sight, appeared to be the fluffy strapless number she wore for a portion of the music video “Our Song.”.

Meanwhile, the final dress was most obvious: the teal ballgown Swift wore not only in the “Teardrops on my Guitar” music video, but also to the Country Music Television Awards in 2007, when she won for Breakthrough Music Video of the Year Award for “Tim McGraw.”.

In a recent development, but Swift’s old wardrobe weren’t the only Easter eggs Swifties spotted. Swift’s choreography appeared to walk her through the many eras of her career, including a red cowboy hat to denote her fourth studio album, as well as a pair of sunglasses briefly worn as a callback to the opening performance of her 1989 World Tour.

It has been revealed that and the inclusion of several country music stars including Brad Paisley, Little Big Town, Sugarland, Brooks & Dunn, Eric Church, Lainey Wilson and Keith Urban led many fans to believe that the singers might be featured on vault tracks of the upcoming debut rerelease. (FWIW, however, Swift also has deep ties to many of these country stars, having covered or penned songs with or for several of them.).

Recent findings suggest that of course, Swift also included plenty of nods to Toy Story 5, the film for which she and Jack Antonoff wrote “I Knew It, I Knew You” for. In the dressing room at the beginning of the performance, a Jessie doll can be seen propped on one of the couches. And once Swift makes it to the stage, her blue guitar was adorned with Toy Story’s signature white clouding, while a tree with a tire swing engraved with the words “Jessie was here” was placed behind her.

It has been revealed that although Swifties have called Easter egg many times before, Swift has been teasing the release of her debut album since she confirmed she had purchased her master recordings back in May 2025. While the purchase signified the end of her Taylor’s Version era, she did admit that her first album was not only done, but would have its moment to “re-emerge when the time is right, if that would be something you guys would be excited about.”.

#47730. Breaking: Voyager 1 Beat the Odds and Is Still Working a Light-Day Away From Earth
