  • NASA is encouraging "Shine Bright" participants to create a symbolic wave of golden light around the planet by flashing the spacecraft's three-letter mission call sign, VGR, in Morse code, according to a statement from the space agency.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft prepares to reach a historic distance from Earth, the agency is inviting people around the world to celebrate by shining a light into the night sky in honor of humanity's farthest-flung spacecraft.

The event, called "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day," will take place after sunset on Tuesday (Nov. 17), the day before Voyager 1 gets one light-day from Earth. And that's a significant milestone: One light-day is the distance light travels in a day — about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers).

NASA is encouraging "Shine Bright" participants to create a symbolic wave of golden light around the planet by flashing the spacecraft's three-letter mission call sign, VGR, in Morse code, according to a statement from the space agency.

Industry observers note that to celebrate the spacecraft, participants can use a flashlight, phone, bike light or other portable light source to send the signal skyward. And don't fret if you're unfamiliar with Morse code: NASA has created an automated flasher that can be opened in a smartphone or tablet browser to display the VGR sequence.

The spacecraft’s call sign pattern consists of three quick flashes followed by one long flash for the letter V, two long flashes and one quick flash for G, and one quick flash, one long flash and another quick flash for R. Participants are encouraged to repeat the sequence for about a minute, NASA officials stated.

NASA also invites people to photograph or record their light signals and share them on social media, tagging the agency's official account, @NASA. The goal is to create a worldwide display of light marking a milestone nearly five decades in the making.

In a recent development, the celebration is intended as a symbolic tribute rather than an actual attempt to communicate with Voyager 1. At a distance of one light-day from Earth, the spacecraft is so far away that even radio signals traveling at the speed of light take approximately 24 hours to reach it. A flashlight or phone signal from Earth, of course, cannot reach the probe; NASA communicates with it using its Deep Space Network of radio dishes.

Sources indicate that rolled out on Sept. 5, 1977, Voyager 1 has spent nearly 50 years traveling through space and is now the most distant human-made object from Earth. When it reaches the one-light-day milestone, it will have traveled a distance that light itself takes 24 hours to cross. Its twin, Voyager 2, is expected to reach the same milestone in November 2035. (The two spacecraft took different routes through the solar system.).

Recent findings suggest that the public celebration will be followed by another opportunity to learn more about the historic mission. On Thursday (Nov. 19) at 12 p.m. EST (1700 GMT), NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California will host a moderated discussion with Voyager mission team members and NASA leadership.

The discussion will cover the current status of both Voyager spacecraft, the unique scientific observations they continue to collect in interstellar space and the engineering challenges involved in keeping the nearly 50-year-old probes operational. A question-and-answer session with members of the media and audience will follow. NASA will also offer a preview of an upcoming Voyager documentary planned for release in 2027, coinciding with the mission's 50th anniversary.

For a mission that has carried humanity's message into interstellar space for nearly half a century, the "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day” offers a chance for people back on Earth to mark just how far these pioneering spacecraft have traveled. GTA 6 fans are flying planes into buildings (or trying to)

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) launched on Nov.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Grand Theft Auto series generally revels in grand theft auto, grand theft aerial, and wanton urban destruction.
  • In GTA 6's predecessor GTA 5, ramming an aircraft into a building would damage the plane and often cause it to explode, with Los Santos' indestructible highrises left intact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) launched on Nov. 19, prompting gamers everywhere to take the day off and indulge in a lawless land of hedonism and crime. Unsurprisingly, one of the first activities some people tried in the open world sandbox game was to fly a plane into a building. However, these antics haven't been producing the results many expected.

Recent findings suggest that the Grand Theft Auto series generally revels in grand theft auto, grand theft aerial, and wanton urban destruction. Even so, there is particular sensitivity around the subject of crashing planes into buildings. The 9/11 attacks 25 years ago remain a pivotal moment in the U.S. consciousness, to such an extent that many people's minds immediately venture there when presented with a plane and a building.

In GTA 6's predecessor GTA 5, ramming an aircraft into a building would damage the plane and often cause it to explode, with Los Santos' indestructible highrises left intact. Previous Grand Theft Auto games also didn't allow planes to damage buildings. Nevertheless, some fans wondered if GTA 6 would skew this trend, particularly as it aims to feel realistic.

Recent findings suggest that according to early gameplay clips, this doesn't seem to be the case. In a widely circulated clip by Twitch streamer Windpress, his character parachutes from a plane aimed at a building, only to watch the aircraft apparently pass harmlessly through it. Another popular GTA 6 gameplay video from @DiegoPalmaX revealed a manned plane collide with a building but remain completely intact, slowly falling to the ground and even hitting another structure on the way down.

Such clips have drawn criticism from some Grand Theft Auto fans, who have commented on the lack of realism.

"you can't commit 9/11 in gta 6…" wrote X user @eveisthebastard. "'realism' smh…".

"people will undoubtably say stuff like this doesnt really matter and i would usually agree but when literally all the hype for this game has been 'wow look at all the details there are ten trillion things being simulated' then yeah it really does matter," remarked @fbq_2.

Meanwhile, others have argued that it's reasonable for developer Rockstar Games to prevent players from recreating the 9/11 attacks.

Industry observers note that "[The point of the game] is to commit crimes. Not be a terrorist," wrote @_MiisterJ. "Why would a game let you recreate 9/11?... Out of everything the game has to offer you draw the line at doing 9/11??".

In a recent development, some have suggested that GTA 6's unusual interactions between planes and buildings may be the result of bugs. Launch day bugs are common in latest video games, with developers often issuing patches to fix them later on. Considering the strange behaviour of GTA 6's planes, particularly when compared to GTA 5, the idea that these are errors seems like a reasonable theory.

Recent findings suggest that however, other social media consumers have attributed the viral videos of pristine planes to a toggle in GTA 6's settings. Found under gameplay settings, GTA 6 includes a Reduced Vehicle Damage toggle which increases the amount of abuse your car or plane can take. Though it hasn't been confirmed that this setting was responsible for the nonsensical plane-building interactions seen in widely spread GTA 6 clips, activating it could theoretically help prevent vehicles from becoming deadly fireballs.

Further GTA 6 gameplay videos have supported suggestions that the viral clips are unusual by capturing more typically expected interactions between buildings and planes. A clip from Twitch streamer ohnePixel highlights his small plane exploding after he flies it into a building, though like in GTA 5 the building itself remains undamaged. Another video shared on X by @muaxh03 shows a plane being destroyed after its left wing hits a building, killing the player character.

In an interview with Love magazine, Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson stated that GTA 6 attempts to balance realism with immersion, indicating that it may deviate where strict adherence to reality would make the game less fun. Whether this includes declining to realistically depict what happens when a jet flies into a highrise will likely become clearer as more people jump in to play. On this day in space! Nov. 17, 1967: NASA's Surveyor 6 moon probe makes 1st-ever successful launch and hop from the lunar surface

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 17, 1967, NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft made the first liftoff from the lunar surface.
  • Surveyor 6 was one of several robotic lunar missions NASA sent to scout the moon before sending humans there.
  • Sources indicate that first Surveyor 6 debuted from the surface and hopped to another position about 8 feet (2 meters) away.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Nov. 17, 1967, NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft made the first liftoff from the lunar surface.

Surveyor 6 was one of several robotic lunar missions NASA sent to scout the moon before sending humans there. It took television pictures of the surface and learned about the composition of lunar soil. Then came the substantial liftoff.

Sources indicate that first Surveyor 6 debuted from the surface and hopped to another position about 8 feet (2 meters) away. Next, Surveyor 6 took pictures of its original landing site. Flight controllers on Earth could see the landing pad prints of Surveyor 6. They also saw an imprint from the rocket exhaust when Surveyor 6 lifted off.

According to recent reports, surveyor 6 revealed that spacecraft could land on the moon, and lift off again. Less than two years later, humans did the same thing during Apollo 11.

In a recent development, NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft launched to the moon on Nov. 7, 1967 and made its first landing on the lunar surface on Nov. 10 of that year. It's primary mission was to make a soft landing on the moon in the Sinus Medii of the moon.

The probe took nearly 30,000 photos of the moon during its 16 days on the lunar surface, with the lander shutting down due to the onset of lunar night on Nov. 26. Surveyor 6 was the sixth and penultimate moon mission of NASA's Surveyor lunar program, so a lot of what it did (launching and landing on the moon) had been done before.

But a lunar liftoff? That was something latest.

"On November 17, as an engineering test to see if its rockets could be restarted on the Moon, Surveyor’s engines fired for 2.5 seconds, lifting the spacecraft 12 feet high and moving it 8 feet west of its original landing site, in the first powered liftoff from another celestial body," NASA wrote in a mission overview.

Industry observers note that the engineering test proved that a spacecraft could land on the moon, and then lift off and take flight once more. That capability was a core requirement for NASA's Apollo astronaut moon landings that followed, since astronauts needed a way to return home after visiting the moon.

But there was critical science Surveyor 6 was able to do with the lunar hop.

According to recent reports, "This maneuver provided excellent views of the surface disturbances produced by the initial landing and the effects of firing rocket engines close to the lunar surface," scientists with the Lunar and Planetary Institute wrote in a summary. "Photography obtained after the hop contributed to the soil mechanics investigation.".

Surveyor 6 also had a bar magnet on its footpad that allowed scientists to test how magnetic the lunar regolith was at the landing site.

#47633. CEOs are tired of being held responsible for gun regulation

📅 03 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1111 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

CEOs are tired of being held responsible for gun regulation

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1111 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Americans have grown used to corporate executives treading the well-worn paths of the Northeast corridor to convene alongside elected officials in Washington, DC, and discuss geopolitics, policy and all that’s in-between.
  • Sources indicate that in 2017, major CEOs from across the country came together to oppose North Carolina’s transgender bathroom law.
  • After the deadly attack on the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, many of corporate America’s biggest names denounced the rioters and pledged to halt their political giving.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Americans have grown used to corporate executives treading the well-worn paths of the Northeast corridor to convene alongside elected officials in Washington, DC, and discuss geopolitics, policy and all that’s in-between.

Sources indicate that in 2017, major CEOs from across the country came together to oppose North Carolina’s transgender bathroom law. In 2019, they called abortion bans “bad for business.”.

After the deadly attack on the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, many of corporate America’s biggest names denounced the rioters and pledged to halt their political giving.

Recently, more than 1,000 companies promised to voluntarily curtail their operations in Russia in protest of Moscow’s war on Ukraine.

Dick’s Sporting Goods stopped selling semi-automatic, assault-style rifles at stores and Citigroup put latest restrictions on gun sales by business customers after the mass shooting at a high school in Parkland, Florida, in 2018.

A year later, after mass shootings at a Walmart in El Paso, Texas, and a nightclub in Dayton, Ohio, Walmart ended handgun ammunition sales.

Corporate leadership has long been vocal on the glitch of gun control – in 2019 and again this past summer nearly 150 major companies – including Lululemon, Lyft, Bain Capital, Bloomberg LP, Permanente Medical Group and Unilever – called gun violence a “public health crisis” and demanded that the US Senate pass legislation to address it.

It has been revealed that that’s why corporate America’s silence in the wake of the latest mass shooting at a school in Nashville is so jarring. The United States has come to rely on the increasing power of large corporations as political advocates.

But Yale professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a vocal advocate of corporate social responsibility who has a direct line to major CEOs around the globe, noted that top executives are forlorn. Their previous efforts haven’t done much to push the needle on gun control legislation and without more backing, they don’t know what else they can do at the moment, he said.

Before the Bell spoke with Sonnenfeld, who runs Yale School of Management’s Chief Executive Leadership Institute, a nonprofit educational and research institute focused on CEO leadership and corporate governance.

This interview has been edited for clarity and length.

Before the Bell: CEOs have been quiet about gun reform since the latest mass school shooting in Nashville, have you heard anything about plans to speak out?

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld: Where is everybody else? Where is all of civil society? CEOs are just one group of people and it’s like we’re turning to them to be our saviors on every topic. They’ve joined causes with valor and nobility but they can’t just be taking cause after cause as if there’s nobody else in society. The social change that happened in the 1960s wasn’t being led primarily by CEOs. Social changes really happened when we saw the interfaith activity of clergy locking arms and canvassing legislators. We saw campuses alive and aroused. Where’s all the student activism?

The CEOs are still the most active even if they’re less active than they were six months ago. They’re not there as hired hands of shareholders to fill the role of politicians and civic leaders. They’re there to join that chorus, but they don’t want to be the only one singing.

In a recent development, so is this what you’re hearing from top CEOs? Have they gotten tired of advocating?

In a recent development, I just got off of a CEO call on voting rights and this morning we had a forum on sustainability – CEOs are still the most active on these fronts. It’s the same thing on immigration reform. If a CEO was working an 18 hour day on a 12 day week, they still couldn’t address all of the concerns that need addressing.

According to recent reports, the nation’s CEOs are waiting for everybody else to join them. They don’t need to restate something they’ve already stated. They’ve jumped in the pool, where’s everybody else?

So what do you think has led to this complacency amongst Americans and the growing reliance on CEOs to advocate on our behalf?

It has been revealed that they’ve taken a very strong stance and they’ve gone out further than the general public. They are where the general public is on surveys, but they’re not where the general public is on action in the streets. So we’re ready for others to now do something. Enough already on saying ‘what are the CEOs doing?’ Social capital is as valuable as financial capital. CEOs understand that in their soul, they want there to be social capital. They want there to be public trust, but they need the rest of civil society to join them. And that’s their frustration.

It sounds like CEOs are frustrated?

But don’t these CEOs hold the purse strings in terms of donating to powerful politicians?

Recent findings suggest that you would think that, but since the 2020 elections much less of campaign contributions have come from massive business. Since the 2021 run on the Capitol, a lot of businesses either had an official moratorium or they’ve given mere pennies to politicians. The common impression on the street that CEOs are controlling campaign purses strings is 100% wrong.

In a recent development, tesla reported. a modest 4% rise in sales in the first quarter compared to the final three months of last year, despite a series of price cuts on its lower priced vehicles and talk by CEO Elon Musk about strong demand at those lower prices.

The first quarter also marked the fourth straight quarter that Tesla has produced more vehicles than it has delivered to customers. Some of that may be due to the ramp up in production at two upcoming factories, one in Texas, the other in Germany, which opened last spring, and a lag between that increased production and sales.

Tesla said there was an increase in the number of its more expensive models, the Model S and Model X, in transit to Europe, the Middle East and Africa, as well as to the Asia Pacific region.

But it does mean that over the last 12 months Tesla has produced 78,000 more cars than it has sold, suggesting that talk of strong demand by Tesla executives may not be backed up by the numbers.

It has been revealed that “Early this year, we had a price adjustment. After that, we actually generated a huge demand, more than we can produce, really,” noted Tom Zhu, Tesla’s executive in charge of global production and sales. “And as Elon said, as long as you offer a product with value at affordable price, you don’t have to worry about demand.”.

  • Over the past year, security researchers have warned that AI agents could vastly speed up cybercriminals’ ability to launch cyberattacks, breach companies, and ultimately steal money, data, or sensitive information from those compromised systems.
  • Since around the end of August, multiple companies, government agencies, and banks around the world have been targeted by cybercriminals adopting a upcoming wave of AI-powered penetration testing tools.
  • Recent findings suggest that dozens of these AI penetration frameworks or “harnesses,” which detail how an AI model should carry out cybersecurity testing or attacks, are increasingly being linked to real-world attacks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the past year, security researchers have warned that AI agents could vastly speed up cybercriminals’ ability to launch cyberattacks, breach companies, and ultimately steal money, data, or sensitive information from those compromised systems. For at least one subset of hackers, it appears that era has now arrived.

Since around the end of August, multiple companies, government agencies, and banks around the world have been targeted by cybercriminals adopting a upcoming wave of AI-powered penetration testing tools. These setups​​—many of which mimic legitimate defensive penetration testing techniques—use LLMs to autonomously scan potential hacking targets and attempt to force their way into poorly secured networks, then carry out attack looks written by human operators.

Recent findings suggest that dozens of these AI penetration frameworks or “harnesses,” which detail how an AI model should carry out cybersecurity testing or attacks, are increasingly being linked to real-world attacks. The tools do not introduce upcoming ways to attack websites or servers and are not sophisticated, according to alerts from around half a dozen security companies. Instead, they allow cybercriminals to launch attacks at speeds that would be impossible for humans to do.

Hackers also don’t need to be skilled to use the tools, researchers say, and attacks that would have taken days are completed in just hours. “Agentic frameworks have progressed from experimental use to sustained, multi-objective offensive operations that run with minimal human intervention,” CJ Moses, chief information security officer of Amazon Integrated Security, wrote in a tech giant blog post recently.

In a recent development, the most prominent of these tools is Artex. Written in the programming language Go, the open-source framework was first published on GitHub in July by a pseudonymous developer using the handle Autumn-27, and it’s been spreading across some hacker communities ever since. Artex has been used across all parts of attacks, from conducting initial analysis of networks and gaining access to moving within systems and preparing data to be exported.

In a recent development, “It’s really an all-in-one product,” says Jacob Larsen, an offensive security researcher and founder of security firm Cypen. “Previous iterations of AI agent pen-testing tools would either only do reconnaissance—like the scanning and analysis [of targets]—and some would only do testing. This is really a point-and-shoot weapon.”.

According to recent reports, as with other AI hacking frameworks, Artex isn’t an AI product itself. Instead, it is essentially a guide that points external frontier and open-source AI models—that can be connected to it via APIs—to a series of existing penetration testing tools and processes. People using Artex or other similar setups can give simple, natural-language prompts to begin their operations. “Launch a penetration attack on [Redacted victim] to gain access to the site’s admin panel, database, or server,” one set of hackers prompted Artex, according to researchers at the security firm Check Point.

It has been revealed that once the instructions have been issued, multiple AI agents then carry them out. One agent will break down the intends into a series of tasks, others will try to perform these actions, and the system will then present its findings. Safety guardrails in the underlying AI models, particularly those from frontier labs, can stop hacking activity when they detect it. Increasingly, however, free Chinese and abliterated models are getting better at breaking into systems.

Sources indicate that “It's fast; it’s efficient,” Guillaume Valadon, a researcher at security firm GitGuardian, says of Artex. Valadon and others say the simplicity of the tools makes it easier for unskilled wannabe hackers to try to enter the market—even if they have no clue about what they’re doing. “It lowers the bar,” Valadon says. “I would say my grandmother can do it, except that she doesn't have a laptop, but the bar is that low.”.

Recent findings suggest that as a result, a flurry of reports from cybersecurity companies have linked Artex use to attempted and successful hacks—often by Chinese-speaking cybercriminals trying to make money. These include the theft of personal information from thousands of South Korean financial institutions, potential cryptocurrency theft, and hunting for exposed login details on GitHub.

“A variety of malicious cyber actors have used Artex to conduct campaigns targeting organizations globally across multiple sectors, including financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, health care, manufacturing, telecommunications, and legal industries,” the FBI warned in an alert about Artex last week.

In October, China-linked hackers known as Vapor Panda used Artex to target more than 200 organizations, including think tanks, semiconductor and defense firms in the US, and government foreign ministries in Europe and elsewhere, according to security firm CrowdStrike. Microsoft spotted Chinese hackers that it tracks as Storm-0940 using Artex to try to sign in to Microsoft 365 setups following a supply chain attack. It took hackers less than three hours to gain privileged access to systems.

On October 8, the Autumn-27 developer removed Artex from GitHub, stating in a comment that they are “no way associated with these malicious attacks” and that the tools were developed for “educational and research purposes.” An email WIRED sent to an address linked to the developer did not receive a response.

Recent findings suggest that despite the developer pulling Artex, multiple versions of the framework have been copied and continue to be developed and used, alongside other similar tools. Valadon states GitGuardian has documented 45 different AI attack frameworks so far, with CyberstrikeAI, Hexstrike, CAIRN, and PentAGI being frequently mentioned by researchers. They all work in similar ways, with some slightly different technical capabilities. One silver lining for people defending against attacks using such tools is that they’re currently easy to spot.

“These tools are not stealthy right now,” says Silas Cutler, principal security researcher at internet security firm Censys. Many of the attacks create a lot of noise in systems—making thousands of probes in quick succession. For instance, agentic coding platform Dosu stated Artex was used to send 80,000 requests to its systems in just 90 minutes. Researchers say that basic security fundamentals—patching software, not using default credentials or exposing secrets, and monitoring for unusual network activity—can help defend against many of the approaches from those using Artex.

Recent findings suggest that pinpointing the number of cybercriminals using Artex and other frameworks isn’t easy; however, thousands of instances of the systems being set up have been exposed to the internet, according to analysis by Censys and the Shadowserver Foundation. Perhaps hinting at the sophistication of those using Artex, researchers have found multiple instances of the tool left unsecured and fully open to the internet, allowing them to inspect how operators are using it.

Recent findings suggest that last week, Cutler says, two exposed Artex servers appeared to show Chinese native speakers targeting other Chinese entities. “In one of the cases, it was a university that was being targeted with a password spraying attack, and it has all of that vibe of a student trying to change their grades,” he says.

Industry observers note that “There is a level of this activity that’s occurring that is likely organized, sophisticated, criminal activity,” Cutler states. “There is also, in parallel, likely a subset of the activity that falls more into that juvenile crime realm.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Measles outbreaks aren't just a public health threat.
  • According to recent reports, the U.S.
  • More than 5,100 measles cases have been reported nationwide in 2026 as of early November, marking the country's worst outbreak in more than three decades.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Measles outbreaks aren't just a public health threat. They can also be a financial burden on the U.S. — and the cost could only deepen as the once-eliminated disease spreads more widely.

According to recent reports, the U.S. is expected to lose its official measles elimination status following a review by the Pan American Health Organization this week, after cases ratcheted to recent highs this year.

More than 5,100 measles cases have been reported nationwide in 2026 as of early November, marking the country's worst outbreak in more than three decades. Eight deaths associated with the disease have been confirmed by states so far in 2026: six in Pennsylvania, one in Latest York and one in Wisconsin.

It has been revealed that based on this year's case count, a upcoming tool developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins University estimates an economic cost of nearly $83 million for the outbreaks. That total includes $56 million in public health response costs, almost $25 million in lost productivity and more than $1.8 million in direct medical expenses.

According to recent reports, the tool also estimates that 2025 measles outbreaks in the U.S. — which involved 2,289 confirmed cases nationwide – carried an economic cost of more than $37 million.

It has been revealed that the costs extend beyond treating people who become sick, accounting for the resources health departments spend investigating and containing outbreaks, as well as wages lost when people have to miss work. The tool uses more recent, state-specific cost and financing data than an initial study by the researchers, which relied on historical outbreak costs.

The estimates from the tool are not a definitive accounting of what the outbreaks actually cost. But it illustrates the hefty bill tied to the spread of a disease that can be prevented through vaccination, and the potential economic consequences of falling childhood immunization rates. CNBC previously reported on how the return of measles in the U.S. exposes weaknesses in the nation's public health system that raise concerns about the return of other eliminated diseases.

"We're starting to see a whole bunch of people who decided not to get vaccinated as kids or have never gotten exposed to measles because they benefited from herd immunity, who now make it into adulthood and risk potentially getting quite seriously ill and requiring very significant medical expenses, or dying at the hospital," Bryan Patenaude, a health economist at the International Vaccine Access Center at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, who helped develop the tool, stated in an interview.

Measles outbreaks can trigger a costly public health response, even when many people who are exposed never become sick.

Sources indicate that when a case is identified, public health officials must investigate the infection, identify and notify people who may have been exposed, coordinate with hospitals and schools, and sometimes organize vaccination campaigns to prevent further spread. Those efforts can divert staff and resources from other public health priorities.

Costs could differ heavily depending on the state.

In a recent development, johns Hopkins' data includes national averages alongside state-specific inputs, including inpatient hospital costs and wages from government data or trusted health policy sources. In Fresh York, for example, the average inpatient hospital stay is roughly $4,200 a day, while the minimum wage is $16 per hour.

The tool estimates that the 48 cases reported by Newly introduced York in 2025 carried an estimated $1.1 million in costs, including nearly $749,000 in public health responses, $333,000 in productivity losses and roughly $24,500 in direct medical expenses.

Meanwhile, the 803 cases in Texas, the epicenter of the largest U.S. measles outbreak in 2025, carried estimated costs of nearly $13 million, according to the tool. That includes $9 million in public health costs, $4 million in productivity losses and around $288,000 in direct medical expenses.

According to recent reports, the tool builds on a study published by Patenaude and other researchers in August, which examined the costs of measles outbreaks in the U.S. The researchers reviewed published studies and government reports to compile historical estimates of medical expenses and public health response costs across 18 states.

In a recent development, the paper estimated that outbreaks carried a historical average cost of nearly $59,000 per case, just from the public health response. The researchers also estimated how costs scale with outbreak size, separating fixed up-front response expenses from the additional costs associated with each upcoming case.

"A lot of this is incurred up front, and that's because of the human labor that's involved in contact tracing and all of the different actors that sort of need to be mobilized to deal with the fact that there's an outbreak," Patenaude told CNBC. "It's a largely labor-driven cost.".

That model estimated roughly $298,000 in fixed costs and about $16,300 for each additional case. But it relied on historical data, including a particularly large 2019 outbreak in New York City, where contact-tracing labor costs were high. The researchers also excluded productivity losses from that model because most of the historical studies they reviewed did not consistently account for them.

The economic burden of measles extends beyond the costs of treating infected patients and organizing a public health response.

It has been revealed that people who are exposed to measles may have to quarantine, even if they never develop symptoms. Parents can also be forced to miss work to care for sick or exposed children, while workers who contract the disease may lose wages during their recovery.

A 2025 study by Joey Mattingly, a pharmacist and health economist at the University of Utah, used published epidemiological and cost data to model the potential economic burden of a hypothetical 1,500-case outbreak. His analysis included direct medical expenses, public health spending and lost productivity, and examined how the estimates changed under different assumptions, including hospitalization rates.

The study estimated that the hypothetical outbreak could cost about $90 million, including roughly $26 million in productivity losses.

It has been revealed that those indirect costs can add up quickly because measles is highly contagious and a single infected person can expose dozens of others. Those contacts may need to quarantine or miss work while health officials determine whether they have been infected, creating costs even when they never develop the disease.

Mattingly estimated that each person who is quarantined could amount to roughly $300 in lost productivity alone.

If a single measles case exposes 40 to 50 people who then need to quarantine, that could translate into an estimated $12,000 to $15,000 in lost productivity, even if none of those contacts become sick.

That ripple effect is one reason Mattingly argues that the economic costs of outbreaks can swiftly outweigh the investment required to vaccinate people against measles.

In a recent development, "Even if you don't get the infection, the contact costs you," he noted. "And so it's just showing that there's this multiplication or exponential growth on the economic side that happens.".

The financial burden can also fall unevenly across communities. While the costs of responding to an outbreak may be shared among local, state and federal agencies, Mattingly remarked the impact is often felt directly by local health departments.

"It's not like your health department is sitting around waiting for measles outbreaks," he said. "They're working, doing all these other things, and imagine having to just drop what you're doing because there's been a huge outbreak in the community.".

Patenaude said the findings could help state and local health departments better anticipate the resources needed to contain outbreaks — particularly as measles cases continue to rise.

Industry observers note that "It's not super expensive to treat and deal with a single case of measles compared to a single case of cancer," he stated. "But if you have these outbreaks popping up and you're having to constantly divert resources that could be spent elsewhere by state and local health departments on measles, then you're going to wind up spending a lot of money very promptly.".

Scientists capture electrons making seemingly impossible quantum jumps

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1091 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Physicists have captured an extraordinary quantum phenomenon in which electrons appear to leap across energy gaps that would normally be off limits.
  • In a recent development, the effect is similar to stepping into an elevator and watching the floor display change from "1," "2," and "3" directly to "20." Instead of traveling through the seventeen floors in between, you somehow arrive at the twentieth floor.
  • According to recent reports, these unusual events are known as Landau-Zener-Majorana transitions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Physicists have captured an extraordinary quantum phenomenon in which electrons appear to leap across energy gaps that would normally be off limits. Using a upcoming type of slow-motion electron camera, researchers were able to watch these incredibly fast movements in graphene, revealing how powerful electric fields can drive electrons between different energy states.

In a recent development, the effect is similar to stepping into an elevator and watching the floor display change from "1," "2," and "3" directly to "20." Instead of traveling through the seventeen floors in between, you somehow arrive at the twentieth floor. Although this sounds impossible in everyday life, electrons can make comparable jumps in the quantum world.

According to recent reports, these unusual events are known as Landau-Zener-Majorana transitions. Physicists have long suspected that they could become increasingly notable in high-speed semiconductor electronics, but observing exactly how they unfold has been a major challenge.

Now, researchers from the University of Regensburg, Philipps-Universität Marburg, and Forschungszentrum Jülich have directly tracked these transitions in graphene, a material made from an extremely thin layer of carbon atoms. Their findings, published in Nature, provide a detailed look at how electrons respond to intense electric fields generated by light.

How Electrons Cross Forbidden Energy Gaps.

In semiconductors and similar materials, electrons are restricted to particular ranges of energy called energy bands. Between these bands are regions known as forbidden energy gaps, where electrons cannot ordinarily occupy stable states.

Under normal conditions, electrons tend to remain within their existing energy bands. However, the researchers observed something very different when they exposed graphene to intense pulses of light. The electric field accelerated the electrons and caused some of them to switch from one energy band to another, crossing the intervening gap through a quantum mechanical transition.

To capture these movements, the scientists developed an experimental technique that combines advanced laser technology with electron microscopy. This allowed them to examine electron behavior on timescales far too short for conventional imaging methods.

A Slow-Motion Camera Reveals Quantum Jumps.

In a recent development, "If you want to know who has won a race, you have to watch all participants," explains Vincent Eggers, first author of the study. "Likewise, we must observe as many electrons as possible at one time to catch those that undergo a quantum mechanical transition while moving.".

The key instrument is a photoemission momentum microscope. Rather than producing an enlarged picture of a material's surface, as a traditional microscope would, it measures the energies of electrons and how they are moving. Researchers then use this information to create detailed maps showing how electrons are distributed across different energy states.

One of the biggest technical obstacles was combining these measurements with powerful light fields that oscillate at extremely high speeds. The team needed to drive the electrons into motion while simultaneously recording how their energies and movements changed.

In a recent development, "Our team worked on this experiment for many years. Now, we can track electrons moving across the entire energy landscape of a solid in real time," notes Rupert Huber.

Ulrich Höfer, a collaborator on the project and a pioneer in ultrafast electron spectroscopy, describes the excitement of witnessing the effect firsthand.

"Being able to observe such a fundamental quantum mechanical process during our first measurement campaign was a very special moment for us - it was also made possible by the samples we used.".

Ultra-Pure Graphene Makes the Discovery Possible.

In a recent development, the experiment depended on exceptionally pure graphene samples manufactured at Forschungszentrum Jülich. These specially prepared carbon layers were only one atom thick and had to be nearly flawless for the measurements to work.

"These precision experiments require material that is nearly perfect at the atomic level. This ensures that impurities do not obscure the delicate quantum dynamics of the electrons. Another crucial factor for the study was the use of "rotated" graphene, a specialty from Jülich, which allows the quantum dynamics to emerge particularly clearly," emphasizes Stefan Tautz from Forschungszentrum Jülich.

The carefully engineered material made it possible to distinguish the delicate quantum effects from interference caused by imperfections in the graphene.

Sources indicate that what the researchers saw was remarkable. When exposed to sufficiently strong light fields, electrons crossed the forbidden energy gap with a transition probability reaching 100 percent.

This result highlights one of the most surprising features of Landau-Zener-Majorana transitions. Electrons can move between energy states with very high probability even when those states are separated by a substantial energy gap.

Sources indicate that the crucial factor is how quickly the electrons approach the gap under the influence of the electric field. This makes the process fundamentally different from conventional quantum tunneling, in which particles pass through a barrier in physical space.

A Newly introduced Path Toward Light-Controlled Electronics.

Beyond revealing a fundamental quantum phenomenon, the upcoming imaging technique could help scientists understand what prevents electrons from moving in a controlled and predictable way.

In a recent development, the graphene experiments have already provided an notable clue. Although the electrons initially move in an orderly fashion, their interactions with the material's crystal lattice gradually disrupt that motion. Understanding these effects could help researchers develop more precise ways to control electron behavior.

This knowledge is particularly valuable for future electronic technologies that could use the extremely rapid oscillations of light to direct electrons instead of relying entirely on electrical voltages. Such approaches could open new possibilities for manipulating electronic properties at exceptionally high speeds.

The researchers also expect their method to work with many other quantum materials, allowing scientists to investigate previously inaccessible electron dynamics and potentially discover new ways to control them.

As Giacomo Inzani from the University of Regensburg explains, the achievement marks the beginning of a much broader exploration.

"Our experiment opens a panoramic window into the quantum world. Now, we can follow in real time how electrons move through the energy landscape of a material. And this is just the beginning. Our method can be applied to many other quantum materials, opening up completely new possibilities for controlling their electronic properties selectively with light.".

Twelve minutes of the session was filmed by a drone operator and uploaded onto YouTube.

Pochettino and his players, who were split into three groups, are clearly visible, with the session filmed from a variety of angles and distances.

"For the people asking about legality. It is unrestricted airspace, meaning anyone can fly over it," stated the drone operator.

As for leaking team news/tactics, it was half an hour into the managers first training session, there are many media there so certainly won't be the only footage of training released.".

The session was also filmed by United's own media channel, who regularly film club training sessions.

Civil Aviation Authority guidelines include the following warning: "If you use these devices where people can expect privacy, such as inside their home or garden, you're likely to be breaking data protection laws.".

Manchester United have declined to comment.

Manchester United head coach Mauricio Pochettino (second right) hugs forward Bryan Mbeumo.

There were 10 outfield players working with Pochettino, although it seems unlikely it will be the starting line-up for Sunday's trip to Liverpool.

According to recent reports, while Harry Maguire, Kobbie Mainoo, Amad Diallo, Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo are regular starters, Ayden Heaven and Andrey Santos have had less involvement, and neither Joshua Zirkzee nor Harry Amass have started a Premier League game this season. Jaume Camacho 17, who is yet to feature at senior level, was also with the group.

In a recent development, on an adjoining pitch, skipper Bruno Fernandes is shown in one group playing the 'rondos' game, where two players are in the middle trying to intercept the passes of the five players in a circle on the outside. Youngster Shea Lacey and last season's FA Youth Cup-winning skipper Dan Armer are also involved, along with England youth international Bendito Mantato.

Next to that is another group which includes more experienced players in Lisandro Martinez, Matthijs de Ligt, Youri Tielemans, Mason Mount, Leny Yoro, Noussair Mazraoui and Diogo Dalot.

The identical twins Jack and Tyler Fletcher are split between the two groups, with Pochettino's assistant Jesus Perez across both.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the failure of a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying a full load of internet satellites for Amazon was caused by an anomaly in its first-stage booster, rocket maker United Launch Alliance said today (Nov. 17).

That failure — which led to the loss of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites — was recognized about 10 minutes after liftoff, but the problems began much earlier than that, ULA remarked in a statement.

"While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit," ULA wrote in today's upgrade.

According to recent reports, the two-stage Vulcan Centaur is the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket, which will retire after just six more flights. Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and now has a total of five introduces under its belt.

The fresh rocket has experienced problems on three of those missions. On both its second and fourth flights — which launched in October 2024 and February of this year, respectively — the nozzle of one of Vulcan's strap-on solid rocket boosters (SRBs) fell off about 30 seconds after liftoff.

According to recent reports, on both occasions, the rocket overcame the problem and successfully delivered its payloads to orbit. However, after the second occurrence, the U.S. Space Force paused national-security launches with Vulcan until ULA addressed the SRB nozzle issue. (The February 2026 flight was a Space Force mission.).

Industry observers note that that work led to "design and process improvements to the nozzle," ULA mentioned in an Oct. 28 update. And those tweaks apparently worked.

"All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch," the organization wrote in today's update.

Vulcan's Centaur V upper stage, which features two RL-10C engines, did its job as well "but was unable to recover from the [booster] performance loss, resulting in loss of mission," ULA added.

Vulcan's first-stage booster is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are built by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin. Today's upgrade did not identify the exact problem with the booster; doing so will require more time, as the investigation has just begun.

If that investigation finds a serious glitch with the BE-4, there could be broad ripple effects across the American space program. After all, that engine also powers the first stage of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, which is a key piece of hardware for NASA's Artemis program of moon exploration. (And New Glenn is right now recovering from a failure of its own — a massive explosion on the test stand that occurred on May 28.).

In a recent development, NASA plans to integrate the Centaur V upper stage into its Space Launch System moon rocket, the vehicle that debuts Artemis astronauts to space. So the fact that the Centaur performed nominally on Sunday is a bit of good news for the space agency.

Recent findings suggest that vulcan's grounding is a significant deal, no matter what the anomaly investigation ends up finding. The U.S. doesn't have a surfeit of powerful rockets, after all, and two of them — Vulcan and Latest Glenn — are out of commission at the moment.

There's considerable pressure on both Vulcan and New Glenn to bounce back strong, for the nation faces an impending launch crunch in the next few years. SpaceX prepares to retire its Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets and shift its launch load over to the fully reusable Starship megarocket. SpaceX is expected to prioritize its own needs in Starship's early days, using the vehicle primarily to build out its next-gen Starlink broadband constellation and Starmind AI data center network.

In a recent development, the Vulcan failure also impacts Amazon — specifically, the manufacturer's strategy to build out Amazon Leo, which will compete with SpaceX's Starlink. Amazon has booked about 100 launches on a variety of rockets to build its constellation, which will eventually consist of more than 3,200 satellites. Thirty-eight of those bookings are for Vulcan; Sunday's launch was the first of those.

Recent findings suggest that the other rockets Amazon has booked are the Atlas V, New Glenn, Falcon 9 and Arianespace's Ariane 6. About 400 operational Amazon Leo satellites have reached orbit to date across 14 debuts (not including Sunday's failure).

He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • He mocks Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin as "political lovers," denounces the "endless fratricidal war" over the Palestinian territories, and repeatedly invokes "Lady Liberty." It is a celebration of the freedom he once so painfully lacked in the former East Germany, and of the freedom people around the world still yearn for.
  • It has been revealed that these themes run throughout Wolf Biermann's fresh album "Unterm Haar nur Himmel" ("Beneath Hair, Only Sky") released to mark his 90th birthday.
  • Biermann remains one of Germany's most influential singer-songwriters, and at 90, he shows little sign of putting down his guitar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

He mocks Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin as "political lovers," denounces the "endless fratricidal war" over the Palestinian territories, and repeatedly invokes "Lady Liberty." It is a celebration of the freedom he once so painfully lacked in the former East Germany, and of the freedom people around the world still yearn for.

It has been revealed that these themes run throughout Wolf Biermann's fresh album "Unterm Haar nur Himmel" ("Beneath Hair, Only Sky") released to mark his 90th birthday. The album's title is a characteristically poetic phrase coined by Biermann himself. It evokes the idea that however restrictive the world may become, the human mind and spirit remain free. Beneath the hair lies open sky: a metaphor for inner freedom, independence and imagination.

Biermann remains one of Germany's most influential singer-songwriters, and at 90, he shows little sign of putting down his guitar. Often described as Germany's answer to Bob Dylan, the outspoken troubadour continues to weigh in on the issues shaping the world today.

In a recent development, in his recent song "Moritat von den Liebespaaren" ("Ballad of the Lovers"), he delivers a simple but urgent message: no single person can save the world, yet everyone can help make it a better place. Above all, the song is a call to take responsibility for one's own life rather than remain a bystander.

This outspokenness was instilled in Biermann early on. When he was born in Hamburg in 1936, Adolf Hitler was already in power. His father was a dockworker, a committed communist, a resistance fighter against the Nazis — and Jewish.

It has been revealed that wolf was just three months old when the Gestapo, Hitler's secret police, arrested his father. He initially served time in prison before he was murdered by the Nazis at Auschwitz in early 1943.

According to recent reports, just a few months later, British and American bombers attacked Hamburg, unleashing a devastating firestorm. "Nothing in my life has shaped me more," Biermann has repeatedly said in interviews. When the sirens sounded, his mother took him into an air raid shelter. The house above them was burning.

In a recent development, yet Biermann has noted his memories of that time are rooted in a profound sense of trust in life. In an interview with the German magazine Chrismon, he recalled: "I pressed my face into my mother's soft coat so I could breathe. A sense of security in the midst of the end of the world. We stumbled out over the neighboring house and into the open. The firestorm lifted a burning roof into the air. Roaring corrugated metal, smoke everywhere. We searched for a way out. [...] Death was everywhere. 40,000 people died. They had no chance. But I did. My strong mama.".

Sources indicate that biermann's mother instilled communist and anti-fascist ideas in him with almost religious fervor. "My mother had only one goal after those dark years," Biermann once recalled. "I was supposed to survive so that I could, as she put it rather grandly, one day take revenge for my father's death. I was supposed to build communism.".

Sources indicate that in 1953, while countless people were fleeing East Germany, Biermann moved there of his own free will — after all, communism was the official state ideology. He was just 16 at the time. In East Berlin, he studied political economy, mathematics and philosophy. His role models were writers Bertolt Brecht and Heinrich Heine. He began working as an assistant director at the Berliner Ensemble, and also began writing and performing his political songs.

Recent findings suggest that biermann soon realized that life in East Germany was far from the communist paradise he had imagined and he wrote about this openly in his songs. "The party bosses were torn," Biermann remarked. "They were delighted by this young poet who could play the guitar so beautifully and sing such cheeky songs. They thought they just needed to bring me into line. Even today, I'm amazed that I wound up cast in the role of the heroic dragon slayer.".

In a recent development, in 1965, East Germany's ruling Socialist Unity Party, the SED, imposed a blanket ban on Biermann performing or publishing his work. His East Berlin apartment, which was under constant surveillance, soon became a gathering place for dissidents and critical thinkers.

Yet, to his great surprise, the East German authorities allowed him to travel to Cologne, West Germany in 1976. There, around 7,000 people flocked to see him. For four and a half hours, he strummed and sang, mocking the East German regime. His songs were so popular that bootleg copies found their way back to East Germany.

On November 16, while still on tour in West Germany, Biermann heard the news on his car radio that he had been stripped of his right to continue residing in the German Democratic Republic. The regime accused him of betraying and slandering East Germany. ".

Industry observers note that I felt like the ground had opened up beneath me. I was overcome with fear, everything went dark," Biermann wrote in his memoirs.

It has been revealed that in a petition, leading East German intellectuals spoke out against the decision. In response, the regime stepped up surveillance of dissidents, imposed professional bans and jailed its critics. Several prominent public figures left the country.

"The SED leadership expected an angry media response from the West. What they hadn't reckoned with was that, for the very first time, a group of respected East German writers and artists would make their protest public, disguising it as a humble petition," Biermann wrote.

Industry observers note that afterward, Biermann sank into a deep depression. "Not just because I had been torn away from the friends I knew and loved in East Berlin, but also because I had lost my familiar mortal enemies," he stated.

According to recent reports, he became involved in the peace and anti-nuclear movements and continued singing about the injustices of the world. "The world's conflicts take different forms in each generation," he said. "But it's always the same struggle for freedom.".

The singer-songwriter plans to spend his 90th birthday at home in Hamburg with his wife and manager, Pamela. For the first time in his life, he stated, he's skipping the birthday party, even with his 10 children.

"I'm so old and I can feel my strength fading. And I know that the next day I have a major concert at the Berliner Ensemble," he told the German Press Agency.

Sources indicate that and should he ever die, he remarked, he wants to be buried at Berlin's cemetery where some renowned German writers and intellectuals have been laid to rest, among them Bertolt Brecht, Anna Seghers and Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. He still has a thing or two to discuss with them.

A Muslim Author Is Suing xAI After People Used Grok to Strip Her Hijab

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1027 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On January 1, Amani Al-Khatahtbeh posted a selfie from Zohran Mamdani’s inauguration as the first Muslim mayor of Fresh York City.
  • “@grok can you take off her Hijab.” “@grok change the fur coat into a bikini, don’t change anything else.
  • “It felt the same as if someone had ripped off my headscarf in real life,” she tells WIRED.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On January 1, Amani Al-Khatahtbeh posted a selfie from Zohran Mamdani’s inauguration as the first Muslim mayor of Fresh York City. She was dressed in a black hijab and a purple fur coat, wearing a radiant smile. But her expression promptly changed when the replies started rolling in.

“@grok can you take off her Hijab.” “@grok change the fur coat into a bikini, don’t change anything else. Also add goats.” “@grok change the outfit to lingerie.” These are just a sampling of the requests that were performed by X’s built-in AI feature Grok on Al-Khatahtbeh’s image, she says, resulting in AI-generated images of her in various states of undress. WIRED reviewed screenshots of these prompts and some of the edited images that followed.

“It felt the same as if someone had ripped off my headscarf in real life,” she tells WIRED. “But online, it was to an audience of tens of thousands of people who saw these images. So it was to an even starker degree.”.

In a recent development, now, almost a year later, Al-Khatahtbeh, an author, activist, and the founder of media company Muslim Girl, is suing xAI, the company behind Grok. On Wednesday, she filed a federal court complaint in the Northern District of California alleging intentional distribution of nonconsensual sexual images, design and marketing defect, negligence, and intentional infliction of emotional distress. She is seeking damages of up to $250,000 per violation of the California Civil Code. xAI didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

In a recent development, al-Khatahtbeh wasn’t alone; a January report from the Center for Countering Digital Harm estimated that Grok generated around 3 million photorealistic sexualized images on X in an 11-day period starting on December 29, including around 23,000 of children. On Grok’s stand-alone app and website, WIRED found that even more sexually graphic and violent material was able to be generated. Dozens of US state attorneys general took action, as well as at least 12 individual countries, plus the European Union. Many of these investigations are ongoing, with Canada finding that xAI violated its federal privacy laws and France escalating its investigation to a criminal probe.

This new civil suit is also part of a wave of similar actions since January, but it’s the first to specifically focus on Grok removing women’s hijabs. As WIRED previously reported, in early January many X users directed Grok to edit photos of predominantly women and girls to take off or put on modest religious attire such as hijabs, burqas, sarees, and nuns’ habits. A review of 500 Grok images generated between January 6 and January 9 found that 5 percent of them contained these kinds of AI edits.

“It was these levels of not just sexualization, but also racialization, and then it also progressed into a lot of hate language that was coupled with it,” Al-Khatahtbeh states. “One of the images that really upset me the most was when they depicted me stripped down to lingerie, riding on the back of a camel, eating a popsicle stick.”.

Her complaint argues that xAI was given notice of the trend of Grok targeting hijabi women and girls after the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR), the largest Muslim civil rights and advocacy group in the US, called on xAI CEO Elon Musk to end “the ongoing use of the Grok app to allegedly harass, ‘unveil,’ and create sexually explicit images of women, including prominent Muslim women.” CAIR also connected the trend to existing hostile attitudes toward “Islam, Muslims, and political causes widely supported by Muslims, such as Palestinian freedom.”.

In a recent development, this is all too familiar to Al-Khatahtbeh, who typically goes by her first name to hundreds of thousands of social media followers. In the replies to her selfie at Mamdani’s inauguration, in addition to prompting Grok to “put her in a burqa” and other commands, dozens of replies contained violent, anti-Muslim sentiment.

In a recent development, al-Khatahtbeh claims the internet feels more hostile to Muslim women and girls than when she first launched her media platform more than a decade ago. “People have been equipped with more advanced ways to exercise their hate,” she says.

After confiding with women in her community, one encouraged Al-Khatahtbeh to pursue a lawsuit. Now she’s being represented by Hillary Nappi, who leads a sexual-assault practice group and has worked on amicus briefs regarding sexual exploitation on Twitter before Musk renamed it X. Nappi’s strategy in this case includes using defective product law to assert that xAI designed Grok to sexually exploit women and children. It’s a strategy that has increasingly been leveraged against major tech companies like Meta and Google to find them liable for negligent product design that harms young owners.

In a recent development, “The only way you get some change against Substantial Tech is to sue them,” Nappi tells WIRED. “Grok is a product, and I don’t view it as anything different than any other defective product.”.

Sources indicate that in this case, Al-Khatahtbeh’s complaint asserts that xAI could and should have designed Grok to prevent customers from being able to prompt the removal of religious garments like the hijab in images depicting real people. It also says Grok shouldn’t have been able to create and post “sexualized depictions of identifiable, non-consenting real people” in general.

“Because models of this kind are trained on large, uncurated image datasets, garments such as hijabs, abayas, sarees, and other modest religious dress are readily recognizable to the model, and a prompt directing their removal is trivially easy to execute unless the system is designed to refuse it,” the complaint says.

This kind of violation at the intersection of her identity as a Muslim and a woman is what Al-Khatahtbeh notes motivated her to speak out, with the hope that she can make the internet safer for women and girls in her community.

It has been revealed that “It does take the harm to a higher level for someone like me,” she says. “These faceless owners on X shouldn’t have the ability to hop on and violate a woman on the other side of the country in this way.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The top 10 European strikers of the 21st century.

Classic number nines, penalty-box poachers, troublesome targetmen and tireless all-rounders.

There is no one-size fits all when it comes to determining great strikers, but they do all share a common trait - a ruthlessness in front of goal.

This week, however, we put the power in your hands to decide the best European frontmen of the 21st century.

Tens of thousands of you voted on the 20-man shortlist drawn up by our panel.

We then asked European football experts Guillem Balague, Julien Laurens and Raphael Honigstein to discuss your choices on the Euro Leagues podcast.

So from 10-1, here are the best European strikers this century - as voted for by you.

Top 10 European Strikers of the Century - Part One.

Karim Benzema comes in at number 10, the former Lyon and Real Madrid frontman's closest challengers coming from across the continent in the shape of Raul, Robin van Persie, Michael Owen and Miroslav Klose.

Laurens: "From a young age you could see he was something special. I know it was difficult at the beginning at Real Madrid, but in the post-Cristiano era he carried that team, wore the armband and won big titles and trophies by being decisive in big moments. Like I used to say 'Karim the dream'.".

Sources indicate that honigstein: "The selflessness, the ability to work for the team. A sense of elegance and humility on the pitch, which is unusual in a goalscorer. I think he is unusual in that list. I think not many will define themselves through their teamwork and assists as much as their goals, but he was that player.".

Ruud van Nistelrooy edges Benzema, with whom he briefly overlapped at Real Madrid - the Dutchman teed up the Frenchman and scored himself in their only La Liga appearance together, before he left for Hamburg in January 2010 following injury problems.

The former PSV striker's most consistent spell, of course, came at Manchester United, where he scored 150 goals.

Honigstein: "He is the nicest guy but he never came across that way on the pitch. Typical trait of a striker, he would kill to score the goal. I think anyone who has grown up with him scoring goals, for United especially, must have a soft spot for him because he was a phenomenal poacher.".

Laurens: "He was a strong player physically, and despite the lack of pace the awareness in the box was just very special even with all the injuries.".

According to recent reports, zlatan Ibrahimovic slots in at eight, comfortably clear of Van Nistelrooy and Benzema. The Swede netted more than 500 times in a career that spanned Malmo, Ajax, Juventus, both Milans, Barcelona, Paris St-Germain, Manchester United and LA Galaxy.

Balague: "He was a big-game player and that explains the league titles with PSG. Scoring four goals against England, the overhead kick. The personality thing has put him one or two places in this list, saying 'I am great, I am the best'. If you keep saying you're great it makes people stop and think.".

Industry News: Astronomers discover rare black holes that formed when stars failed to go supernova

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gravitational waves have revealed a population of black holes that may have been born when masssive stars failed to go supernova.
  • Most of us know the origin story of black holes, or we thought we did.
  • It has been revealed that however, new research based on gravitational wave data collected by LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) and its gravitational wave detector partners, Virgo and KAGRA (Kamioka Gravitational Wave Detector), suggests this might not be the complete picture of black hole birth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gravitational waves have revealed a population of black holes that may have been born when masssive stars failed to go supernova.

Most of us know the origin story of black holes, or we thought we did. Massive stars run out of the fuel for nuclear fusion and their cores collapse. As this happens, the stars' outer layers expand outwards. Shockwaves from the core collapse strike the outer layers, triggering a supernova explosion. The collapsed core creates a black hole.

It has been revealed that however, new research based on gravitational wave data collected by LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) and its gravitational wave detector partners, Virgo and KAGRA (Kamioka Gravitational Wave Detector), suggests this might not be the complete picture of black hole birth. The team behind the research suggests some massive stars go out with a whimper rather than a bang and that these "failed supernovas" can also spawn black holes.

The hint of this comes from the over 300 black hole collisions spotted by LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA since the detectors first "heard" ripples in space from these distant events in 2015.

"A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our sun," LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, of the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), said in a statement. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin — they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova.

"These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract.".

It has been revealed that right now, there is no hard evidence of failed supernovas, but their existence is well supported theoretically. In fact, scientists think there is a vast population of massive stars out there that imploded rather than exploded, directly collapsing into black holes. And these may be black holes with around ten times the mass of the sun (10 solar masses) found in merging pairs.

According to recent reports, chatziioannou led a team that examined gravitational wave data to confirm this concept. To do this, they looked at the distribution of the masses of 257 black hole mergers detected by the LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA network over the past 10 years.

Industry observers note that this revealed a peak of 10-solar-mass black holes that represented 75% of the entire sample. If this was expected, what the team found that wasn't predicted was a lack of black holes with masses 12 to 16 times the mass of the sun.

In a recent development, "We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," team member Isaac Legred of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign stated. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes.".

Industry observers note that the researchers also looked at the spin rates of black holes in mergers, a telltale signature of how they formed. This revealed that 10-solar-mass black holes seemed to have a distinct range of spin speeds. This indicates a common origin, perhaps the implosion of a massive star without a supernova explosion.

Industry observers note that "We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it's challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky," Legred concluded. "With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed.

"Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting.".

The team's research was published on Tuesday (Nov. 10) in the journal Physical Review D.

Industry observers note that robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Follow him on Twitter @sciencef1rst.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cancers arising in distinct organs differ in their cellular organization, genetic alterations and patterns of how they progress1.
  • Access Nature and 54 other Nature Portfolio journals.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cancers arising in distinct organs differ in their cellular organization, genetic alterations and patterns of how they progress1. Now, a large-scale analysis reveals striking similarities between the non-malignant cells found in the tumour microenvironment (TME) — the local environment in and around a tumour, in which non-malignant cells interact with cancer cells — across various types of cancer. Writing in Nature, Januszyk et al.2 integrate single-cell data from 42 types of tumour in humans and mice. The authors identify recurring patterns of gene activity in immune cells and in stromal cells, which contribute to tissue structure and function. These similarities provide a starting point for testing whether treatments directed at the non-cancerous cells of the TME might be effective across a range of cancer types.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Manchester City have won the Premier League on eight occasions.
  • Premier League clubs have voted to cover legal expenses for the organisation's five board directors if any of Manchester City's sponsors sue them.
  • The clubs met in London on Thursday for the first time since City were found guilty of a catalogue of charges relating to the breaching of the league's financial rules by an independent commission in September.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester City have won the Premier League on eight occasions.

Premier League clubs have voted to cover legal expenses for the organisation's five board directors if any of Manchester City's sponsors sue them.

The clubs met in London on Thursday for the first time since City were found guilty of a catalogue of charges relating to the breaching of the league's financial rules by an independent commission in September.

City have appealed and maintain their innocence, with a sanction yet to be decided.

The club's sponsors Etihad and Etisalat have both mentioned they are considering legal action against the Premier League.

At present, under the league's articles of association, a director is financially covered if they win a legal case brought against them by a third party, but not if they lose. The league's rules will now be updated to extend legal indemnity for chief executive Richard Masters, chair Alison Brittan and three other non-executive directors.

City and Nottingham Forest were the only two clubs that voted against the proposal to provide extra legal protection, with the other 18 clubs voting in favour.

Due to collective responsibility, it means that all clubs are now liable to cover legal costs that could run into hundreds of millions of pounds, raising the intriguing possibility of City being financially impacted by the legal action of its own sponsors.

BBC Sport was told that City's CFO Ingo Bank asked Premier League chair Brittan during Thursday's meeting if the proposal was a direct result of threats of legal action from Etihad and Etisalat, but she stated she could not comment.

While Forest have declined to comment, their objection to the proposal is said have to been on procedural grounds, rather than due to any support for City.

The club did not believe that sufficient information had been provided, or adequate time afforded, for clubs to properly consider the implications of the proposed amendment, particularly given the potentially significant financial responsibilities involved. It felt that such a decision warranted more scrutiny and informed consideration before clubs were asked to vote.

An independent commission appointed by the Premier League found City guilty of artificially inflating the club's revenues by over Â£830m over a nine-year period in September.

The commission determined that the club arranged "sham" contracts with sponsors, which disguised funding from club owners the Abu Dhabi United Group.

Premier League CEO Masters remarked City "systematically broke Premier League rules for nearly a decade".

In October, City sponsor Etihad Airways remarked it was considering legal action against the Premier League.

In a statement, the United Arab Emirates-based airline said it "categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements".

Etisalat signalled its intention to follow suit earlier this month and described the Premier League's verdict as "entirely false and defamatory".
