📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hollywood is mourning the loss of a veteran actor.

It has been revealed that larry Poindexter—best known for starring in the 2003 film S.W.A.T.—died on Nov. 18, his rep Adam Levine confirmed to E! News. He was 66.

“Larry was someone who was incredibly kind and loving to his family, friends and strangers alike,” Levine said. “A true artist who was devoted to his craft, Larry took great joy in entertaining and informing through his performances.”.

Poindexter died four days after being struck by a car in Los Angeles, according to NBC News, citing police and the late actor's agent Harry Gold.

Poindexter—who shared twin sons with his wife Carol Kritzer—had been picking up food in his Studio City neighborhood on Nov. 13, before he was hit by a car while crossing the street, per the outlet.

Recent findings suggest that the General Hospital alum was subsequently hospitalized and was set to undergo surgery for his broken ribs on Nov. 18, but he died suddenly, according to Gold.

Poindexter’s agent told NBC News that doctors did not believe his injuries were “anything serious,” adding, “They put him in the hospital for observation and to repair some broken bones and then he passed away.”.

Along with his role as LAPD Captain Tom Fuller in S.W.A.T., Poindexter, who had nearly 200 acting credits throughout his career, was also known for his stints on soap operas Days Of Our Lives, Santa Barbara and General Hospital. He also held a recurring role on the '90s legal drama JAG.

In more recent years, he appeared on The Hard Times of RJ Berger. His costar on the MTV comedy Paul Iacono was among those who expressed their grief after Pointdexter’s untimely death.

“I’m heartbroken by the loss of Larry Poindexter, my dad on RJ Berger,” Iacono wrote in a Nov. 19 Instagram post alongside throwback photos with his on-screen dad. “Few people I’ve known were as kind, generous, fiercely talented, and f--king hilarious. Above all, Larry was a GOOD egg.”.

The 38-year-old shared that Poindexter “looked out” for him in his early 20s, writing that he “offered wisdom I wasn’t always ready to hear,” and “taught me that being a good person and collaborator mattered just as much as being a great actor.”.

As he concluded his emotional post, Iacono emphasized that he’ll never forget his time sharing the screen with Poindexter.

“I’m forever honored to have played his son,” he wrote, “and I’ll always cherish him as my second father.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, fossils provide an extraordinary window into Earth's distant past, revealing the animals, plants, and ecosystems that existed millions of years ago.
  • As a result, our picture of prehistoric life is filled with major gaps.
  • In a recent development, to help solve this problem, Thomas A.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, fossils provide an extraordinary window into Earth's distant past, revealing the animals, plants, and ecosystems that existed millions of years ago. Yet the fossil record tells only part of the story. Fossilization is exceptionally rare, meaning that just a tiny fraction of the organisms that once lived on Earth have been preserved. Even when fossils survive, scientists can only discover them if the rock layers containing them are accessible today.

As a result, our picture of prehistoric life is filled with major gaps. Some geological periods and parts of the world have produced abundant fossils, giving scientists a detailed understanding of the life that existed there. Other periods and regions remain largely unexplored. Because fossil excavations require considerable time and resources, knowing where to search could make a major difference in uncovering newly introduced evidence of ancient life.

In a recent development, to help solve this problem, Thomas A. Neubauer of the Bavarian State Collections of Natural History (SNSB) and Mathias Harzhauser of the Natural History Museum in Vienna have developed a new tool for guiding fossil research. The two paleontologists analyzed the geographic distribution of fossil discoveries from animals that inhabited shallow marine environments over the past 540 million years. For the first time, they also mapped the regions of the world where fossil information is missing, providing a clearer picture of where future discoveries may be possible.

Mapping 540 Million Years of Ancient Marine Life.

In a recent development, to build their map, the researchers examined records from the Paleobiology Database (PBDB), the world's leading freely accessible repository of fossil information. The database contains a substantial portion of the paleontological findings published by scientists around the world.

Recent findings suggest that using these records, the team reconstructed where fossils from ancient shallow marine environments have been documented throughout Earth's history. They also examined how fossil research has developed over decades and centuries, measuring how frequently investigations in different regions have produced latest scientific information.

The researchers then compared these findings with geological information from the Macrostat database. This allowed them to assess not only where fossils have already been discovered, but also where suitable rock formations could provide opportunities to fill key gaps in the fossil record.

Where Earth's Missing Fossils May Be Hiding.

Industry observers note that the analysis revealed a surprising imbalance in our understanding of prehistoric life. The Early Mesozoic (approx. 252 to 66 million years ago) and the Palaeozoic (approx. 539 to 252 million years ago) have already been studied extensively. According to the researchers, additional fossil discoveries from these periods are unlikely to produce a substantial increase in scientific knowledge in the near future.

The greatest opportunities for expanding the fossil record may instead lie in more recent geological history. Although scientists have already collected extensive evidence from the Cenozoic Era (beginning 66 million years ago), the analysis suggests that its shallow marine deposits still contain significant untapped potential for fossil discoveries.

To help researchers investigate this period, the team identified locations around the world where previously unknown fossil species are especially likely to be found. Crucially, these are also places where the appropriate geological layers are exposed or otherwise accessible, making actual discoveries possible.

A Treasure Map for Future Fossil Discoveries.

Industry observers note that by highlighting regions where crucial evidence may still be waiting, the upcoming approach could help paleontologists strategy more productive expeditions and make better use of limited research resources. Rather than concentrating on areas that have already been explored extensively, scientists can focus on locations with the greatest potential to reveal something new about Earth's prehistoric ecosystems.

"The fact that many regions of the Earth remain unexplored offers hope for valuable new discoveries," indicates SNSB paleobiologist Neubauer.

"But precisely because expanding the fossil record is quite challenging and progresses only slowly, our work can help researchers worldwide to focus their research specifically on these still largely unexplored areas. We provide a valuable guide for planning future projects and excavation campaigns. The same applies to the examination of existing museum collections awaiting scientific analysis. Through sensible prioritization, we can fill gaps in the fossil record strategically.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Season 4 is upon us, and we're ready to be dragged back into the creepy woods of teen chaos and middle-aged mayhem.
  • Trailers for Season 4 have teased the titular soccer team's return home.
  • But hey, if the off-season has you feeling foggy on which teammates (and rivals) have bit the dust (or been bit up), we've got you covered with a recap of all the deaths in Seasons 1, 2, and 3.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buzz buzz, Yellowjackets hive! Season 4 is upon us, and we're ready to be dragged back into the creepy woods of teen chaos and middle-aged mayhem. The Season 3 finale offered some major moments, including the revelation of the Pit Girl's identity and Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) sending out a distress call to the civilized world.

Trailers for Season 4 have teased the titular soccer team's return home. However, if the first three seasons have taught us anything, it's that you can take the girl out of the wilderness, but you can't take the wilderness out of the girl. In both the past and present timelines, Shauna (Sophie Nélisse/Melanie Lynskey), Misty (Samantha Hanratty/Christina Ricci), and Taissa (Jasmin Savoy Brown/Tawny Cypress) are grappling for survival and control, so buckle up for a wild ride.

But hey, if the off-season has you feeling foggy on which teammates (and rivals) have bit the dust (or been bit up), we've got you covered with a recap of all the deaths in Seasons 1, 2, and 3.

And keep an eye on this space — the final season of Yellowjackets is sure to see more folks fall, and we'll be updating this list accordingly.

In a recent development, also, wherever possible, we have images with sliders of before and after. Slide 'em if you can stomach it.

Having just moved up from the junior varsity team, Rachel has the grim distinction of being the first Yellowjacket to die. Like the plane's pilots, she died in the crash, from a laceration to her throat.

Sources indicate that father of Travis and Javi, Coach Bill (Carlos Sanz) died as a result of the plane crash that dropped the team in the Canadian wilderness. He'd fallen out of the plane into a tree. In an added bit of brutality, he died in front of Travis, as the teen boy tried to save him from his painful perch in a tree.

In a recent development, good Christian girl Laura Lee (Jane Widdop) died a hero. After the team found an intact plane in the wilderness, Laura Lee began reading the manual to figure out how to fly it. She eventually took off with her teddy bear Leonard — and her personal lord and savior Jesus — as her co-pilots. But the plane exploded in the air, killing Laura and the Yellowjackets' chance of sending out a member for help.

The queen bee who couldn't hack it in the cabin, Jackie (Ella Purnell) froze to death while sleeping outside. And then she had the bizarre honor of becoming the first to be eaten by the team.

Travis's younger brother Javi (Luciano Leroux) would also be eaten, though the Yellowjackets weren't directly to blame for his death. While the team was hunting Natalie, Javi offered her a hiding place. But before they could get to safety, he fell through the ice of a frozen lake and died. From there, he was eaten.

According to recent reports, despite the best efforts of the team, Shauna's baby was stillborn. This was a sad one.

Remember when Misty made a friend? She and Kristen (who was dubbed Crystal the Pistol by the team) bonded in the wilderness over their shared love of music and Steel Magnolias. They grew close enough that Misty shared her secret about destroying the plane's emergency transmitter, which Kristen — understandably — judged. From there, Misty pushed her off a cliff, and proclaimed the girl "missing.".

Real talk: Ben (Steven Krueger) lived way longer than we expected. The plane crash severely damaged his leg, which Misty then amputated on the spot. And incredibly, he survived possible infection, likely starvation, and the burning down of the cabin. But he couldn't escape the Yellowjackets. In a kangaroo court, they convicted him for the cabin's fiery annihilation (despite Misty's best efforts of a defense), and Taissa was chosen to carry out the execution. However, this was not how Ben died. Instead, he was tortured with crippling violence and deplorable conditions — that is, until Natalie took mercy on him and stabbed him fatally in the heart.

According to recent reports, poor Edwin (Nelson Franklin) just wanted to study frogs with his colleague Hannah (Ashley Sutton) and their guide Kodiak (Joel McHale). But then he stumbled in the Yellowjackets camp as they were feasting on Ben's remains. And, well, Lottie welcomed him with an axe to the head. RIP Edwin.

After Edwin was killed, the Yellowjackets imprisoned his surviving friends like they did Ben. When Kodiak tried to escape, he wasn't ended by the girls but by Hannah, who stabbed him in the eye. This was Hannah's bid to show the girls she could be trusted to keep their secret. And it got her through the rest of Season 3 at least.

Yellowjackets began — to quote Sarah McLachlan — building a mystery by introducing the show with the death of the Pit Girl. Underdressed for the snowy weather, she raced through the woods, pursued by masked figures, and ultimately fell into a pit of spikes, which killed her. Season 3 revealed her identity: Mari Ibarra (Alexa Barajas), a persistent rival of Shauna's. Mari too was eaten.

How Travis (Andres Soto) died was a significant mystery in Season 1, with a real bummer of a reveal. In the present, accidentally hanged himself while attempting to talk to the darkness. Lottie was supposed to save him but had a technical malfunction.

According to recent reports, in Season 1, Adam Martin (Peter Gadiot) was a mechanic who was having an affair with Shauna. But when Shauna began to suspect he had betrayed her, she stabbed him to death. His murder was covered up with the help of Misty, Nat, Taissa, and Jeff, because Yellowjackets are ride or die. (Sometimes both!).

Masquerading as a journalist, Jessica Roberts (Rekha Sharma) got on the wrong side of Misty Quigley, who fatally poisoned her with fentanyl-laced cigarettes.

According to recent reports, taisaa's family pet was murdered by Night Taissa. Then, his head was placed on creepy basement altar, which would prove a foreshadowing for Ben's fate.

Recent findings suggest that in Season 2, Detective Kevyn Tan (Alex Wyndham) was put in the awkward position of investigating his former high school classmates as he looked into the disappearance of Adam Martin. When his search led him to Lottie's cult's headquarters, he was felled — not by a Yellowjacket! — but by one of their fans. Specifically, Walter Tattersall (Elijah Wood), a citizen detective who fell for Misty. As the two were talking, Walter subtly poisoned Kevyn with a laced hot cocoa.

Nat (Juliette Lewis) died in the Season 2 finale, and we're still not over it. Of all the survivors, she seemed the one who likely to succeed in escaping their past. Worse yet, she was killed by her friend, Misty.

It has been revealed that it was an accident. Misty was trying to kill one of Lottie's cult members, Lisa (Nicole Maines), but Nat intervened by throwing her own body in front of the syringe, which was filled with poison. However, Natalie's story continued in the flashbacks. And yet, that only promised to make her ending sadder.

In a recent development, who killed Lottie Matthews (Simone Kessell)? Well, to the surprise of many, it wasn't Shauna. It was her daughter, Callie Sadecki (Sarah Desjardins). Sure, Callie and Lottie had bonded, no matter how much that enraged Shauna. But when Callie confronted Lottie about stealing the incriminating DAT tape from the Sadecki home, Lottie began saying cryptic things about how Callie was a child of the Wilderness' darkness. In a rage, Callie reacted by shoving Lottie down the stairs.

Taissa's high school paramour (Liv Hewson) rejoined to the fold to reignite their romance and proved a solid teammate (Lauren Ambrose) in the present timeline. But their bliss was punctured by Van's cancer diagnosis, and yet that was not how she died! Hopeful the whatever of the wilderness would save her if she sacrificed someone else, Van tried to kill Melissa (Hilary Swank), a ball-capped Yellowjacket who was long thought dead, but had resurfaced under weird circumstances.

Ultimately, however, Van decided not kill Melissa. And in response, Melissa fatally stabbed her and fled, leaving Taissa to bury Van in an unmarked grave. Naturally, she took the opportunity to cut her lover open and eat her heart.

How Premier League's substantial six keep getting richer

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ten games into the Premier League season, four of the top five places are occupied by 'significant six' clubs.
  • Only second-placed Brighton, a club with a model which must be the envy of many of their rivals, and Premier League ever-presents Everton, have muscled their way in.
  • In pure financial terms, it should come as no surprise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ten games into the Premier League season, four of the top five places are occupied by 'significant six' clubs.

Only second-placed Brighton, a club with a model which must be the envy of many of their rivals, and Premier League ever-presents Everton, have muscled their way in.

In pure financial terms, it should come as no surprise.

The six biggest clubs - Manchester United, Liverpool, Manchester City, Arsenal, Tottenham and Chelsea - now generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the division's other teams.

Sources indicate that and the gap is growing. Every season.

BBC Sport breaks down how the finances of the significant six have exploded, examines upcoming trends and the impact on the transfer market, and asks how much it really matters.

According to recent reports, companies put their money where supporters are prepared to spend it. It is a simple fact of business in every country, a reality of football's food chain.

In England, Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester United traditionally dominated viewing figures, column inches, shirt sales and sponsorship.

Over the past 20 years they have been joined by Chelsea, Manchester City and Tottenham.

This group of clubs now generate so much money it is hard to imagine how they can fail in the long term - even factoring in short-term performance challenges.

Let's look at how the gap has grown.

We will use Everton, the only club not in the big six to be in the Premier League since its inception in 1992.

This tells a tale of how even one of the league's founding members can be left trailing well behind.

According to recent reports, in 2009-10, the gap in revenues between the major-six average and Everton was Â£120m. In 2024-25, that gap had grown to Â£442m.

So what has driven this huge escalation?

In large part it is the boom in international TV rights.

Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport that it has attracted companies prepared to pay large sums to be associated with the Premier League's top clubs.

"The major football brand clubs have global fanbases and that makes them very attractive to global commercial partners, especially for sponsorship and front-of-shirt deals," Maguire said.

"You combine that with the fact that the Premier League is broadcast to 190 different countries around the world, and especially the international audiences - that allows the clubs to negotiate very good prices.".

Only 10% of Everton's revenue comes from commercial deals, while for the major six it is 45%.

It has been revealed that it means Everton, and other clubs in the league, are heavily reliant on broadcast income. It makes up 66% of their revenue.

For Everton at least, this should change following the move to Hill Dickinson Stadium.

But that is unlikely to be enough to stop the gap increasing.

It has taken a few years, but Aston Villa and Newcastle have begun to increase their revenue.

This is largely thanks to the financial rewards of Champions League football.

But even Uefa has created a system which entrenches the position of the biggest clubs.

When the European Super League plan was torpedoed, Uefa created a latest financial deal called the value pillar.

This reserves 35% of all Champions League revenues, or Â£713m, for the historically most successful clubs.

At the end of the league phase last season City are estimated to have earned Â£37.9m from the value pillar, Liverpool Â£35.5m and Chelsea Â£33.3m. Newcastle received only Â£13.6m.

The good news for Villa is their coefficient has improved greatly, aided by last season's Europa League win.

In a recent development, their value pillar is projected to be worth Â£25m this season. But that will still be less than the big six clubs in the competition.

The cards are stacked against an ambitious club - not just domestically, but in Europe too.

Take a look at the financial trend of the major six and one thing becomes noticeable - Chelsea are beginning to fall behind.

In the past two seasons, and for the first time in recent history, the Blues recorded the lowest revenues of the big six.

Industry observers note that not just by a small amount. They were Â£74m behind Tottenham, and Â£200m below Liverpool and Manchester City.

City's matchday income is the lowest, with the club's huge revenues largely due to commercial deals.

City, however, have been found guilty of breaching the Premier League financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18, inflating the value by using "sham contracts" with sponsors.

The club deny wrongdoing and have lodged an appealed against the verdict.

Chelsea's problem is simple - seats.

Stamford Bridge has a capacity of only 40,000, with no easy scope for expansion. The rest of the major six have grounds which hold at least 60,000.

Chelsea generated an average spend per fan of Â£80 in 2024-25, the second highest in the league after Arsenal.

Yet with 20,000 fewer tickets sold than their major six rivals, Chelsea's total matchday revenues are dwarfed.

In a recent development, "Matchday spend has become increasingly important," Maguire said. "There has been a flatlining of broadcast revenues, especially since 2017.

"As a consequence, clubs have had to look at alternative methods of increasing revenues, especially with costs both on the pitch and off pitch rising so fast.".

Matchday revenue has effectively stalled for Chelsea, rising only Â£16m over the past 10 years. United's has grown by Â£69m and Spurs, thanks to their new ground, by Â£85m.

"Chelsea are far more reliant upon player sales," Maguire noted. "There is a growing divide because the global appeal is very much aligned with three or four clubs.

Sources indicate that "Arsenal have re-established themselves with their progress in the Champions League. Manchester United are a brand in their own right. And Liverpool have expanded Anfield from 44,000 to 61,000, with many of those extra seats having gone to commercial.".

Chelsea's successful player trading model has so far limited the impact.

But there are signs that, financially at least, the significant six could become the big five.

You might recall that Villa and Newcastle were not fans of the old profit and sustainability rules (PSR).

PSR forced both clubs to sell some of their best players to balance the books.

That has changed this season with squad-cost ratio (SCR).

In a recent development, there is a key difference with SCR, in that it allows a club to spend the money they generate on players. PSR limited losses so was more restrictive.

"This does make it a little easier for the likes of Villa and Newcastle to spend money," Maguire said. "But it is still heavily weighted in favour of the major six.

"SCR is different to PSR rather than better. For some people, change is advantageous. For others, it isn't.".

The major six generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the other clubs. So they can spend hundreds of millions of pounds more on their squads.

This makes the big six even more powerful in the transfer market.

"Look at the clubs who voted against SCR - Brighton, Brentford, Bournemouth, Crystal Palace, Fulham and Leeds," Maguire said.

"It's very noticeable that those clubs have traditionally been very good at player sales, while they have tended to have lower matchday and commercial revenues.".

Most of the substantial six - the outlier being Chelsea - are not remotely close to the Premier League's 85% SCR limit.

If you give clubs more money to spend on transfers, the likelihood is they will do just that. And the numbers back that up.

Premier League clubs spent Â£3.5bn - not only a highest total for a summer window, but it almost smashed the record for a whole season, the Â£3.53bn set in 2025-26.

The annual accounting cost of previous transfers, or amortisation, has been rising year on year.

"Over the course of the last decade, transfer amortisation has more than doubled and close to tripled," Maguire said.

"Which means that on average, clubs in the Premier League are now spending, or now have a cost which goes into their SCR calculations of just under Â£100m.".

Uefa fears that SCR will make matters worse, and have an inflationary impact across Europe.

And you can see why it is concerned.

In the summer 13 Premier League clubs broke their transfer record.

Brentford, Brighton, Palace, Leeds and Nottingham Forest all spent more than Â£40m on a player - unthinkable until recently.

So we have learned that the major six have more money than ever, and the gap is so huge it is impossible for any other club to compete with them, financially at least.

And this is an important point: other than Villa and Newcastle, the other clubs are not trying to compete with the big six.

Clubs like Brentford and Brighton have shown that smart models are just as effective as fat wallets.

They sign the potential stars of the future, nurture them and then sell them to the significant six.

Football's ecosystem recycles the big-six money through the transfer market.

But it is a precarious business for these other clubs.

"The smaller clubs have to get it right on a more regular basis than the bigger clubs," Maguire said.

"The big six can afford to make signings which are Â£60m and Â£70m, who turn out to be relative flops, and still have those players on high wages for several years.".

And this is perhaps the key point about the vast finances of the massive six.

Sources indicate that the commercial power of the big six does not guarantee success. After all, United sit in the relegation zone.

Yet Mauricio Pochettino, their upcoming manager, may well get the chance to revamp the squad despite the club spending Â£945m on players in the past five years.

According to recent reports, the richest clubs can try to spend their way out of trouble. Again and again.

But the rest of the league are only a couple of bad transfer windows from catastrophe.

And that is the real gap between the significant six and the rest.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress made her first address to the staff on Wednesday and just minutes into the meeting told employees that they can expect pay raises and more equity in December, months ahead of schedule, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED.
  • “So I’m here to tell you, the best thing that we want to do is to take care of each and every single employee that is here and to make sure that you feel good about this company and you do not worry about your comp,” she stated.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress made her first address to the staff on Wednesday and just minutes into the meeting told employees that they can expect pay raises and more equity in December, months ahead of schedule, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED.

“So I’m here to tell you, the best thing that we want to do is to take care of each and every single employee that is here and to make sure that you feel good about this company and you do not worry about your comp,” she stated.

Industry observers note that questions about compensation were the most common among the 700 submitted ahead of the meeting, Kress stated. She said the next-most common request was for transparency from the board.

Kress’ comments came during the first companywide meeting following the resignation of Jensen Huang as CEO last week. Huang had led the computer graphics chip maker since cofounding it 33 years ago, and his presentations during the quarterly town halls internally had become a much anticipated and memorable spectacle for some of the company’s nearly 49,000 employees. Information rarely leaked from the meetings in the past. Nvidia declined to comment for this story.

But now Nvidia is facing an extraordinary leadership crisis. Huang resigned amid allegations of extramarital affairs, including potentially with a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia’s board chair Harvey Jones said on Tuesday that Huang disclosed “personal behavior” contrary to the firm’s policies and norms and wouldn’t be invited back.

During the companywide meeting on Wednesday, Jones reiterated that the board accepted Huang’s resignation due to his personal conduct and “lack of candor.” He remarked the tech giant wouldn’t find a “Jensen clone,” but that there are “dynamic leaders out there, with demonstrated intellect, high-tech engineering experience, strategic thinking, cultural compatibility, and a track record of success.” He added, “We will not compromise our requirements for the sake of expediency” and that the board would accept employee suggestions on the CEO search.

Recent findings suggest that thousands of employees have apparently lobbied for Huang’s reinstatement. Several well-known tech executives signed a public petition, with about 200,000 purported backers urging the same. Instead, the board is searching internally and externally for a replacement at one of the world’s most valuable companies and one of the biggest drivers of the generative AI boom.

Recent findings suggest that huang’s departures and a slew of government investigations into him and Nvidia have rattled investors. But on Tuesday, Nvidia reported better-than-expected financial results and forecast growing sales in the years to come. Shares were up about 5 percent on Wednesday.

Recent findings suggest that one concern investors have expressed is whether Nvidia might see a brain drain of top talent. Many employees have stayed at Nvidia for Huang and his vision. Nvidia could also be perceived as a less desirable place for new and emerging talent to work, with its leadership in flux, during an especially critical time as competition in the AI chips market grows.

On Tuesday’s third-quarter earnings call, an analyst from Bank of America Securities asked Kress directly about her “message” to Nvidia investors about talent retention, as well as the tech giant’s overall durability and financial strategy through this major upheaval. Kress replied that “probably the most crucial thing” company leaders are thinking through right now is stabilizing its employee ranks.

Sources indicate that “We are always thinking about our employees. Like every community out there, there are diverse opinions,” Kress noted. “We will take care of our employees during this transition to make sure they are safe and make sure the work can be done in the current environment.”.

In a brief question-and-answer session with Kress during the all-hands meeting Wednesday, Nvidia cofounder Chris Malachowsky addressed how the company could maintain its prized culture going forward.

Recent findings suggest that he recalled how he, Huang, and other cofounders thought it was “nonsense” to put cultural values up on posters. Instead, they want it instilled in “the way you behave, the way you work together, and the way you work,” and he believes that will stand the test of time. “We’re going to be fine,” he said.

Kress ended the meeting, which lasted about 50 minutes, by comparing Nvidia’s employees to “90,000 people packed into the sweatiest, hottest” University of Florida football game.

According to recent reports, in the third quarter, “every single person sings,” she said. “It is impressive to see them all together, all in harmony singing that song … Do you know what? We’re gonna hear that song, guys. And I believe in all of you, that you will help sing it. Nvidia, we’ve got this.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We're in a bit of a cyberpunk revival at the moment. 2026 gave the excellent second season of Netflix’s "Cyberpunk: Edgerunners," and Prime Video's "Blade Runner 2099" is just around the corner. 2027 will continue this trend with "Neuromancer" blasting onto Apple TV.

Based on cyberspace guru William Gibson’s seminal 1984 novel, "Neuromancer" follows Case, a brilliant hacker who falls into a web of digital espionage and crime as he attempts an impossible corporate heist. The pulp noir novel has been hailed as a generational revelation, and its slang and terminology have become ingrained in computer nerd subcultures.

After decades of development hell and failed attempts at various studios, "Neuromancer" and its plugged-in digital dystopia are finally jacking into the small screen in January 2027.

Apple TV is already the secret home of amazing sci-fi, and "Neuromancer" will join the streamer's impressive roster of science fiction stalwarts like "Foundation", "Silo", "Invasion", "Dark Matter", "Murderbot", "For All Mankind", "Pluribus", and "Star City.".

According to recent reports, can it live up to the hype? We won't have to wait long for an answer. In the meantime, let's jack into cyberspace and scour the code for everything we know about Apple TV's "Neuromancer!".

Apple TV+’s Neuromancer officially powers up on Jan 22, 2027.

It was first announced to be in full production back on July 1, 2025, which actually coincided with the 41st anniversary of the publication of William Gibson's absorbing book.

Filming took place in Tokyo, Los Angeles, Istanbul, Canada, and London to create a truly international flair to replicate the novel’s action.

Gibson's "Neuromancer" is a dense, jargon-heavy juggernaut of a book that demands intense concentration to absorb all the slang, lingo, computer terms, and staccato literary rhythms, but it's a fantastic immersion into a fully fleshed-out world. It's also worryingly prophetic, showing a world not unlike ours today in 2026.

"Neuromancer's" TV iteration seems to be following the novel closely and will center around Case, a brilliant, cocky, neurologically damaged hacker who is forced into a logistical quagmire of digital corporate espionage with his cyber-enhanced partner Molly after embezzling cash from an employer.

Sources indicate that molly is a "razor-girl" mercenary with mirrored eyes who dreams of attempting a dangerous heist against a nefarious corporate dynasty hiding deep, dark secrets. Hackers (known as console cowboys) "jack in" to guarded computer systems using sophisticated software and surgically implanted ports to bypass firewalls and security protocols.

In a recent development, molly’s mysterious client is Armitage, a former black ops military operative with a shadowy past. The team’s prime target is a next-generation super AI entity named Wintermute.

Everything goes smoothly until it doesn’t, and Case and Molly are soon running for their lives before eventually coming into contact with Wintermute’s AI sibling, called Neuromancer. A merger of the two systems seems inevitable, and the crux of the narrative is focused on that certainty.

The first cryptic teaser trailer for "Neuromancer" landed back on July 1, 2025, to mark the start of filming.

Sources indicate that revealed in the brief video was a murky cocktail watering hole that springs to life in a flourish of humming lights and tinkling pinball machines. A bright blue-and-orange neon sign blinks on in the back, spelling out the name Bar Chatsubo, the iconic Chiba City hacker lounge that's well known to dedicated readers of the 1984 novel.

A second teaser came on July 6, 2026, in which a retro computer was powered up to display the opening sentence of Gibson’s book, describing the dour atmosphere of Japan's Chiba City... "The sky above the port was the color of television, tuned to a dead channel.".

It's such a classic line that perfectly reflects that bleak cyberpunk mood.

Then, on July 25, 2026, Apple TV released the first full teaser (or short trailer) that revealed much of the series' visual style, the mega-city setting, and the main cast of Callum Turner, Brianna Middleton, and Mark Strong.

It’s got a serious edge and attitude that sets the tone with bold graphics and enticing sounds.

"Neuromancer" was co-created for TV by Graham Roland ("Tom Clancy's Jack Ryan," "Dark Winds") and J.D. Dillard ("Devotion," "The Outsider," "Sleight").

Industry observers note that it’s a 10-episode prestige series collaboration between Skydance Television and Anonymous Content that's also produced by Drake's production company, DreamCrew Entertainment. Graham Roland serves as "Neuromancer's" showrunner, with J.D. Dillard inked to direct the pilot episode and perhaps other installments.

"We're incredibly excited to be bringing this iconic property to Apple TV+," executive producers Roland and Dillard confirmed last year in a statement.

"Since we became friends nearly 10 years ago, we've looked for something to team up on, so this collaboration marks a dream come true. 'Neuromancer' has inspired so much of the science fiction that's come after it, and we’re looking forward to bringing television audiences into Gibson's definitive 'cyberpunk' world.”.

JetBlue unveils fresh first-class seats to bring back profits

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (630 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • JetBlue Airways unveiled its upcoming domestic first-class seats Wednesday as more of the country's carriers bet on the premium travel boom to make them profitable again.
  • JetBlue confirmed it would offer a domestic first class — BlueFirst — in December 2024 and aims to start flying aircraft with the fresh seats and full on-board product next month.
  • JetBlue will have 12 of the seats on its Airbus A320 fleet and 30 extra-legroom seats, down from 42 of those options previously.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

JetBlue Airways unveiled its upcoming domestic first-class seats Wednesday as more of the country's carriers bet on the premium travel boom to make them profitable again.

JetBlue confirmed it would offer a domestic first class — BlueFirst — in December 2024 and aims to start flying aircraft with the fresh seats and full on-board product next month. The carrier demonstrated off the new cabin at its home hub at John F. Kennedy International Airport on Wednesday. Retrofits will continue during 2027, CEO Joanna Geraghty told CNBC late last month.

JetBlue will have 12 of the seats on its Airbus A320 fleet and 30 extra-legroom seats, down from 42 of those options previously. Because the airplanes don't have ovens, JetBlue stated it is offering an array of cold food options like sesame noodles, pastrami sandwiches and tortellini salad, though they vary by route.

Industry observers note that the rollout comes as the New York airline tries to stabilize after last posting a profit in 2019. Last month, JetBlue executives sought to calm investors after shares in the airline hit a record low following a report that bondholders had contracted restructuring advisors.

Sources indicate that "We have no intention, no plans to file for bankruptcy. We are not engaged with any restructuring organization," Geraghty told CNBC in an interview on Oct. 27.

Geraghty told CNBC's Phil LeBeau on Wednesday that JetBlue has "met with a few of the creditors over the last couple of weeks as part of ... normal investor engagement." She said the tech giant made it clear to bondholders that JetBlue doesn't need to reorganize.

The airline's shares are up more than 40% this month, more than other passenger carriers, as of midday Wednesday, though they are still off about 11% so far this year.

JetBlue is betting that resilient travel demand, especially for roomier seats will help fuel its turnaround strategy, which aims to get the carrier to an operating profit next year and $1 in adjusted earnings per share in 2028.

In a recent development, airline executives have stated they expect fares to stay elevated next year as they grapple with higher costs, including but not limited to fuel, such as labor and airport fees. Geraghty said Wednesday that even if fuel prices moderate next year, "I don't think fares are going to fall as much as people expect.".

Airlines large and small are racing to outfit their cabins with roomier, more expensive seating options to help cover ever-higher costs, from jet fuel to labor to airport operation fees.

For example, a ticket in the newly introduced recliner first-class seats between Kennedy airport and Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport in Florida is going for $847 roundtrip in the first week of March while standard economy is $446.

On Tuesday, budget carrier Frontier Airlines unveiled its new first-class seats, which will take up the first two rows, and mentioned it would outfit its Airbus fleet with premium seating that has extra legroom and in-seat power through row eight. The airline will take out a row of seating on its planes to make the pricier ones fit, Chief Marketing Officer Bobby Schroeter told CNBC in an interview Monday.

JetBlue last month reported that it ended the third quarter with $2.2 billion in liquidity and that its unencumbered asset base is now $7 billion, including $2.8 billion in aircraft and engines.

In a recent development, jetBlue had total debt of $8.4 billion as of Sept. 30, the carrier mentioned in its earnings filing.

Geraghty told CNBC last month there is a "fundamental disconnect between the narrative in the bond market and what our financial results actually demonstrate.".

When asked whether JetBlue's eye on keeping costs down includes furloughs, layoffs or buyouts, Geraghty last month said "absolutely not.".

Tech Report: Shevchenko accuses Mudryk camp of 'baseless slander'

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (506 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ukraine great Andriy Shevchenko has accused Mykhailo Mudryk's representatives of repeatedly asking for an employee of the country's football federation to "falsely" take the blame for the winger's positive drugs test.
  • Tottenham winger Mudryk, who is on a season-long loan from Chelsea, was suspended from November 2024 until July 2026 after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium.
  • The 25-year-old said he blames the Ukrainian Association of Football (UAF) for his failed drugs test and subsequent ban, believing it entered his system while on international duty.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mykhailo Mudryk has won 28 caps for Ukraine.

Ukraine great Andriy Shevchenko has accused Mykhailo Mudryk's representatives of repeatedly asking for an employee of the country's football federation to "falsely" take the blame for the winger's positive drugs test.

Tottenham winger Mudryk, who is on a season-long loan from Chelsea, was suspended from November 2024 until July 2026 after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium.

The 25-year-old said he blames the Ukrainian Association of Football (UAF) for his failed drugs test and subsequent ban, believing it entered his system while on international duty.

In an interview on Wednesday, Mudryk firmly placed the blame for his 20-month absence from the sport on his national association, which has led to Shevchenko's response.

In a statement, former Chelsea and AC Milan striker Shevchenko, who is now president of the UAF, mentioned Mudryk's comments amounted to a "baseless slander against our people, who do their work honestly and professionally" and called on the player to retract his words.

He added: "His representatives repeatedly approached the UAF with a proposal to find an employee who would falsely take responsibility for the meldonium found in his doping sample.

"The UAF refused, as such a proposal contradicts the principles of our work.".

He added that "numerous investigations and audits" undertaken as part of the case were unable to shed light on when or where the substance entered Mudryk's system.

In his interview Mudryk also claimed Shevchenko had offered him little support, blamed the association for leaks that emerged during the case and said its handling of the matter delayed his return to football.

However, Shevchenko went on to say that national team staff had complied with a request from Chelsea not to provide Mudryk with any medication while on international duty.

And he also challenged the former Shakhtar Donetsk forward to provide evidence "to back up his words".

"Head coach Serhiy Rebrov also approved for Mykhailo to have two of his personal specialists work with him at the training camps," Shevchenko added.

"These were the exact people who monitored his regimen and recovery, and helped him with his daily routine.

Industry observers note that "The UAF completed all necessary checks in this case. We provided Mudryk's representatives with the information they requested and remained in contact with those working on the case.

"I know the people who have worked with the national team for many years. I trust them, because throughout all this time there have been no incidents in the team that could make anyone doubt their professionalism.

Industry observers note that "If Mykhailo has evidence to back up his words, let him provide it. If no such evidence exists, I expect him to publicly retract his accusations and apologise to the people whose honesty and professionalism he has called into question.".

BBC Sport has contacted Mudryk's representatives for comment.

Mashable offers watch guides for all of the above, broken down by genre: comedy, thriller, horror, documentary, and animation, among others. Darius Rucker rose to fame in the '90s as the frontman of the rock band Hootie & the Blowfish. In the 2000s, he went solo, first in R&B, then country music. Now, he looks back on a journey that included fame, fortune, struggles with drugs and alcohol, a marriage that fell apart, and much, much more.

Directed by Jason Bergh, Darius Rucker: They Called Me Hootie promises fans a look into the life and music that's kept its subject rolling for decades, with more to come. — Kristy Puchko, Entertainment Editor.

How to watch: Darius Rucker: They Called Me Hootie is now streaming on Hulu and Disney+.

It has been revealed that after seven seasons on Netflix, The Circle seemed like it had its last round. However, fans of the popularity-based competition reality show can catch the series in its new home on Hulu, with Season 8 landing this week on the streamer. This time around, the competitors will be both civilians and celebrities, who will vie for ultimate social dominance in the show's apartment block — whether playing as themselves or catfishing the others.

In a recent development, sadly, the Hulu series will not have Netflix host Michelle Buteau, who hosted all seven seasons of the Netflix series. Instead, creator Tinx aka Christina Najjar will have immaculate shoes to fill as the upcoming Circle host. — Shannon Connellan, Senior Editor.

How to watch: The Circle is now streaming on Hulu.

It has been revealed that nicolas Cage is John Madden in a film you can either watch or not — it's your life. The Hollywood star leads American Hustle director David O. Russell's sports biopic, which follows Madden's NFL coaching and commentary career through to the development of EA Sports' Madden games. In particular, the film explores his partnership with Oakland Raiders owner Al Davis (Christian Bale) and the team's first ever Super Bowl victory in 1977. There's football history, ample prosthetics, and Cage-style roaring from the sidelines, so there might be something in here for you. — S.C.

Starring: Nicolas Cage, Christian Bale, Kathryn Hahn, Sienna Miller, John Mulaney, and Shane Gillis.

How to watch: Madden is now streaming on Prime Video.

HBO's latest documentary paints a personal portrait of the people behind Never Use Alone, the confidential, anonymous, volunteer-operated hotline for people using drugs by themselves — people who don't have someone in their life they could (or feel they could) call for help in an emergency.

Sources indicate that written and directed by Ricki Stern and Jesse Sweet, the short documentary speaks to people who have used or volunteer for the U.S. National Overdose Response Spotting service, who alert emergency services to caller locations if they stop responding while using. Notably, the Trump administration has been moving from "harm reduction" approaches to drug use, including restricting federal funding to support overdose hotlines. The Hotline encapsulates why these grassroots programs are so vital. — S.C.

How to watch: The Hotline is now streaming on HBO.

It has been revealed that the collapse of crypto exchange FTX is one of the biggest stories of the tech world in recent years. Now, it comes to Netflix in The Altruists, inspired by Upcoming York Magazine articles by Kevin T. Dugan and Jen Wieczner.

It has been revealed that anthony Boyle plays FTX founder and former CEO Sam Bankman-Fried, while Emmy winner Julia Garner plays Caroline Ellison, CEO of FTX's sister organization Alameda Research. The Altruists examines their relationship, as well as their larger journey from idealists trying to change the global financial system to fraudsters accused of stealing billions.* — Belen Edwards, Entertainment Reporter.

Starring: Julia Garner, Anthony Boyle, Alex Lawther, Karan Soni, Naomi Okada, Madison Hu, Matt Rife, and Eugene Young.

How to watch: The Altruists is now streaming on Netflix.

Industry observers note that the global obsession with Formula 1 will not hit the brakes anytime soon, nor will the women driving to victory in the sport. In a upcoming documentary from Disney+, you'll go behind the scenes of the F1 Academy, the all-female Formula 1 racing championship series rolled out in 2023. The film particularly focuses on the 2025 F1 Academy season, following drivers Maya Weug, Doriane Pin, Alisha Palmowski, and Chloe Chambers through the competition, and giving you a look at what it takes to get on the hallowed F1 track. — S.C.

Starring: Maya Weug, Chloe Chambers, Alisha Palmowski, and Doriane Pin.

How to watch: The Pursuit: F1 Academy is now streaming on Disney+.

English comedian Oobah Butler has mastered the art of the prank. In 2017, he created fake restaurant The Shed at Dulwich, which became TripAdvisor's top-rated restaurant in London, all without serving a single meal. That same year, he "bullshitted" his way to the top of Paris fashion week by posing as a designer. Since then, he's created documentaries about infiltrating Amazon and getting funding for business ventures. This week, he releases a five-part HBO and A24 series, Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow.

According to recent reports, throughout the series, Butler sets up scams aimed to target five different topics: wellness, wine, dating apps that use AI, music, and royalty. Based on the trailer, his ideas range from pitching a serum made of children's tears to communicating via remote control butt plug. If you love Nathan Fielder's Nathan for You business propositions but wish they were even more out there, this is the show for you. — B.E.

Industry observers note that how to watch: Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow premieres Nov. 22 at 11 p.m. ET on HBO and HBO Max.

Though Gentle Monster explores a dark, difficult subject, Léa Seydoux delivers a commanding performance as a woman facing shocking truths in her own family.

Sources indicate that written and directed by Corsage's Marie Kreutzer, the film centres on concert pianist Lucy (Seydoux) — and the film's music, by Camille, is an eclectic pop triumph. Captured with elegance and empathy by director of photography Judith Kaufmann, Lucy's idyllic life with her adoring husband Philip (Laurence Rupp) and young son is shattered when the police (led by an excellent Jella Haase as Detective Elsa Kühn) show up with a search warrant, accusing Phillip of a heinous crime. Forced to reckon with the accusations and view the person she loves through an unthinkable upcoming lens, Lucy will never be the same — and it's within this nuance and emotional complexity that Seydoux thrives. — S.C.

Starring: Léa Seydoux, Jella Haase, Laurence Rupp, Malo Blanchet, Anton Rubtsov, Nils Strunk, Sylvester Groth, Patrycja Ziółkowska, Regina Fritsch, and Catherine Deneuve.

How to watch: Gentle Monster is now streaming on Netflix.

The wrongful conviction of Alfred Chestnut, Andrew Stewart, and Ransom Watkins (the so-called Harlem Park Three) is the focus of HBO's upcoming documentary, When a Witness Recants.

It has been revealed that directed by Dawn Porter and produced by Ta-Nehisi Coates, the film examines the miscarriage of justice that occurred in Baltimore, Maryland, when the three innocent 16-year-olds were sentenced to life in prison for the murder of 14-year-old DeWitt Duckett in 1983. Featuring interviews with Chestnut, Stewart, and Watkins, the film explores the 36 years they wrongfully spent in prison, the failures of the Baltimore Police Department, and their path to freedom and exoneration in 2019. — S.C.

How to watch: When a Witness Recants is now streaming on HBO Max.

American author Patricia Highsmith wrote a string of sensational thriller novels, but she's best known for created Tom Ripley, the killer con man who's spawned a series of adaptations all his own.

In a recent development, in A Talent For Murder, however, the Ripley adaptation gets a new, riveting wrinkle. Helen Mirren stars as Highsmith, who's living in a remote cabin in Switzerland when an ambitious young American man (Alden Ehrenreich) comes calling. He wants her to write another Ripley novel, to appease his publisher bosses back in the states. She wants a mind to mess with, and he's seductively willing. While he romances a beguiling young woman (Olivia Cooke), author and admirer join forces to imagine a fictional scenario worth of Ripley. What's fantasy and what's reality? The lines blur in this sexy and wickedly entertaining film. As I cheered in my review out of TIFF, "A Talent For Murder is darkly funny, freshly thrilling, and unrepentantly seductive. It's not a Ripley sequel, but it's damn close." — K.P.

Starring: Helen Mirren, Alden Ehrenreich, and Olivia Cooke.

How to watch: A Talent for Murder is now available for rent or purchase on Prime Video, Apple TV, and Fandango at Home.

Comedy nerds, you have to see this one.

The full title of this superb documentary from Nick Davis is You Had to Be There: How the Toronto Godspell Ignited the Comedy Revolution, Spread Love & Overalls, and Created a Community That Changed the World (in a Canadian Kind of Way). Its focus is looking back at the 1972 Toronto production of Godspell, which boasted such not-yet-famous performers as Martin Short, Eugene Levy, Gilda Radner, Victor Garber, Andrea Martin, Dave Thomas, Jayne Eastwood, and Paul Shaffer. And most of the above offer interviews, home movies, and personal recordings of this pivotal moment in Canadian comedy.

Recent findings suggest that this movie was one of my absolute favorites at last year's Toronto International Film Festival. And as I cheered in my review, "You Had to Be There gifts audiences plenty of laughs, and so much more. This is not some fluffy celebration of comedians or even Godspell. Davis and company have come together to craft a documentary that is both informative, historical, entertaining, and deeply humane."* — K.P.

Starring: Martin Short, Eugene Levy, Victor Garber, Andrea Martin, Dave Thomas, Jayne Eastwood, and Paul Shaffer.

How to watch: You Had to Be There is now available for purchase on Apple TV and Fandango at Home.

It has been revealed that directed by John Ripa and Alyce Tzue, Steps is a soft-goth twist on Cinderella. Centered not on on the famous princess (Amanda Seyfried) but her so-called evil stepsister Lilith (Ali Wong), this animated adventure offers a tale of rebellion, regret, sisterhood, and magic. The story you thought you know gets a fun shake-up that includes not only a fairy godmother (Bette Midler) and a charming prince (Daniel Radcliffe), but also a chipper talking frog (Stephanie Hsu), a medieval mean girl (Nikki Glaser), and a hot troll (Young Mazino).

Whether you've got a kiddo who's gotten a little too old for the standard Disney Princess fare, or you can't get enough of fractured fairytales, Steps is sure to please. As I wrote in my review, "Cheers to the small army of writers who've earned screenplay and story-by credits on this film (Ava Tramer, James Madejski, Jen Chuck, Dana Schwartz, Felicia Ho, Riki Lindhome, and Kate Micucci). Steps gives audiences a familiar dose of fairy-tale tropes, then uses them to explore topics that can be tricky to explain to kids... But it's through the conflict of two sisters — one privileged and playing by the rules, the other marginalized and defiant — that each learns how to be better and more loving to themselves and each other. And kindness is contagious." — K.P.

Starring: Ali Wong, Amanda Seyfried, Stephanie Hsu, Nikki Glaser, Daniel Radcliffe, Young Mazino, Peter Dinklage, and Bette Midler.

How to watch: Steps debuts on Netflix on Nov. 20.

In its third season, Percy Jackson and the Olympians moves beyond the ground covered by the movies, giving Rick Riordan fans their first onscreen adaptation of The Titan's Curse. That means it's time to give a warm welcome to Bianca and Nico di Angelo (Olive Abercrombie and Levi Chrisopulos), two fan-favorite characters making their screen debuts this season.

The arrival of Bianca and Nico isn't the only major change shaking up Camp Half-Blood this season. Thalia (Tamara Smart) is back, which means Percy (Walker Scobell) is no longer the only child of the Substantial Three at camp. As these two embark on a quest to save a kidnapped Annabeth (Leah Sava Jeffries) and the goddess Artemis (Dafne Keen), will they get along? Or will they turn on one another in a conflict of mythic proportions? Book fans know that The Titan's Curse is where things get dark, so be warned. But don't worry: At least we know we'll be getting dam jokes.* — B.E.

Recent findings suggest that starring: Walker Scobell, Leah Sava Jeffries, Aryan Simhadri, Dior Goodjohn, Daniel Diemer, Charlie Bushnell, Tamara Smart, Olive Abercrombie, Levi Chrisopulos, Dafne Keen, Saara Chaudry, Ming-Na Wen, Hubert Smielecki, Jesse L. Martin, and Holt McCallany.

Sources indicate that how to watch: Percy Jackson and the Olympians Season 3 premieres Nov. 20 on Disney+, with latest episodes weekly.

In a recent development, buzz, buzz! The Yellowjackets are back for their fourth and final season. In past and present timelines, the Yellowjackets are dropping like flies. We can't wait to see how things shake out for Shauna, Misty, Tai, and Melissa. (And Jeff!).

Last season ended with teen Natalie successfully escaping teen Shauna's hunt to use the frog scientist's repaired SAT phone to call for help. But anyone who can count can take a look at the Season 4 trailer and see that not all of residents of Camp Yellowjacket will make it back to civilization. This season we're likely to learn what happened to Hannah and Akilah. But will the show finally reveal the mysteries of the wilderness? What does that symbol mean? And of the still-standing Yellowjackets in the present-day timeline, who'll make it alive to season's end? — K.P.

Starring: Melanie Lynskey, Christina Ricci, Tawny Cypress, Warren Kole, Sarah Desjardins, Hilary Swank, Sophie Nélisse, Sophie Thatcher, Jasmin Savoy Brown, Samantha Hanratty, Courtney Eaton, Liv Hewson, Kevin Alves, Jenna Burgess, and Nia Sondaya.

Sources indicate that how to watch: Yellowjackets Season 4 premieres Nov. 20 on Paramount+.

In a recent development, thanks to Don Bluth, we have magical and thrilling animated adventures like The Secret of NIMH, The Land Before Time, An American Tail, Anastasia, and All Dogs Go to Heaven. Now, documentarians Dave LaMattina and Chad N. Walker take a look back at this American animator's life and works, with the documentary Don Bluth: Somewhere Out There.

In a recent development, the film ushers audiences back to the early days of Bluth's life as a little boy inspired by Walt Disney's groundbreaking animated feature, Snow White and the Seven Dwarves. Then, through archival footage, clips from a variety of animated films — including Bluth's — and interviews with the man himself, Somewhere Out There charts the dizzying highs and devastating lows that seemed to come with every project. There's a story about payments coming in a paper bag that's sure to have you cracking up. But most of all, it's riveting how candid Bluth is, whether recounting his animation company's rivalry with the Disney studio or his own personal struggles.

It has been revealed that A must-see for any true animation lover, Don Bluth: Somewhere Out There is not to be missed. —K.P.

How to watch: Don Bluth: Somewhere Out There is now available on VOD.

Industry observers note that like Odysseus (Matt Damon) landing on the shores of Ithaca after 20 years away, The Odyssey is finally coming home. Christopher Nolan's epic hits digital this week, complete with 90 minutes of bonus features. That means you can watch from your couch (just the way Nolan intended) as Odysseus braves the cyclops Polyphemus, Laestrygonian warriors, and a sniveling Robert Pattinson on his way back to his wife Penelope (Anne Hathaway) and his son Telemachus (Tom Holland). If you purchase the digital edition, you'll also get access to 90 minutes of bonus features.

One of the best films of the year, The Odyssey pushes Nolan to stranger, more grotesque places than ever before, and the result is spectacular. As I wrote in my review, "[Nolan] takes us right into the heart of The Odyssey, fantasy, muck, and all. The result is nothing short of masterful." — B.E.

Starring: Matt Damon, Tom Holland, Anne Hathaway, Robert Pattinson, Lupita Nyong’o, Zendaya, and Charlize Theron.

How to watch: The Odyssey is now available for digital purchase on Prime Video.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, vaccines may do more than protect people from the immediate effects of a viral infection.
  • Scientists at Pompeu Fabra University discovered that mice recovering from an acute viral infection experienced prolonged problems with their immune defenses.
  • In a recent development, most people think of common viral infections, such as colds or stomach viruses, as temporary illnesses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, vaccines may do more than protect people from the immediate effects of a viral infection. New research suggests they could also help prevent lasting damage to the immune system that remains even after the virus has disappeared.

Scientists at Pompeu Fabra University discovered that mice recovering from an acute viral infection experienced prolonged problems with their immune defenses. Although the animals had successfully fought off the virus, their immune systems remained impaired, making it harder to respond to latest threats. Remarkably, mice vaccinated before infection did not develop these problems, suggesting that vaccination may provide an additional layer of protection beyond preventing illness.

In a recent development, most people think of common viral infections, such as colds or stomach viruses, as temporary illnesses. A virus enters the body, multiplies, causes symptoms, and is eventually brought under control by the immune system. Once symptoms disappear, recovery is generally considered complete. The immune response also creates protection against future encounters with the same virus.

But what if the immune system continues to experience harmful effects long after the infection appears to be over?

Viral Infections Can Leave Lasting Immune Damage.

Researchers from Pompeu Fabra University's Infection Biology Laboratory investigated this possibility in a study published in Cell Death & Disease.

It has been revealed that using mice with acute viral infections, the team examined what happened to their immune systems after the animals had recovered. They found that eliminating the virus did not necessarily restore normal immune function. Instead, the infection left behind changes that persisted well beyond the initial illness.

Recent findings suggest that according to Andreas Meyerhans, an ICREA research professor at UPF, who led the research, "there is a general perception that an acute viral infection is a relatively minor and transient event: once the virus is controlled and the symptoms have resolved, the body has fully recovered and is back to normal. But this view may underestimate consequences that are not immediately visible and can persist long after the infection itself has resolved.".

The researchers traced these lingering effects to significant changes in the spleen, an organ that plays an important role in coordinating immune defenses. As the immune system fought to eliminate the virus, the spleen developed fibrosis, a condition involving the buildup of scar-like tissue. The arrangement and positioning of immune cells within the organ also became disrupted.

These structural changes interfered with the interactions between immune cells that are necessary to activate T cells. These specialized cells are essential to adaptive immunity because they help recognize and destroy infected cells.

In a recent development, as a result, the mice remained less capable of launching effective immune responses when exposed to newly introduced challenges. Even though the original infection had been brought under control, their immune defenses continued to function poorly.

In a recent development, "The infection can be controlled, but that does not necessarily mean that the host has fully recovered," indicates Dr. Paula Cebollada Rica, first author of the study. "Our findings show that the immune-related consequences of an acute viral infection can persist beyond the period in which the virus is detectable, leaving the animals in an immunocompromised state.".

Vaccination Prevented Lasting Immune System Damage.

After identifying these long-term effects, the scientists investigated whether they could be avoided. They focused on vaccination, which prepares the immune system to recognize and fight a pathogen before an infection occurs.

The results revealed a striking difference between vaccinated and unvaccinated animals. Mice that received vaccination before infection did not develop the spleen damage or immune dysfunction seen in the other group.

Their spleens maintained their normal structure, and their T cells continued to function at levels comparable to those of mice that had never been infected.

Recent findings suggest that this finding suggests that vaccination can protect the immune system itself from some of the harmful consequences of fighting a viral infection. In the mouse model, vaccination not only protected against the disease caused by the virus but also preserved the animals' ability to respond to future immune challenges.

"Vaccinated animals did not experience T-cell dysfunction or splenic alterations after recovering from an acute viral infection. This means that vaccination not only prevented the disease resulting from the acute infection but also preserved the immune system's ability to cope with upcoming challenges," Cebollada Rica explains.

A Hidden Benefit of Vaccines With Public Health Implications.

The findings broaden the potential benefits of vaccination by highlighting a form of protection that may not be immediately apparent. Beyond reducing the immediate effects of an infection, vaccines may also help prevent persistent changes that weaken immune defenses.

Although these results were obtained in mice and do not establish that the same effects occur in humans, they raise crucial questions about how viral infections influence long-term immune health and how vaccination might help protect it.

The research also comes at a time when vaccination policies and infectious disease prevention efforts are increasingly influenced by political decisions. The researchers emphasize the importance of scientific evidence in understanding the full consequences of infections, particularly when policy choices can undermine coordinated efforts to prevent infectious diseases.

Understanding the broader benefits of vaccination could therefore influence not only medical care but also how public health officials explain the value of vaccines to the public.

"The benefits of vaccination highlighted by this research are important not only for healthcare, but also for how we communicate the value of vaccination to the population at large," Meyerhans states. "It is important that people are aware of the broader protection that vaccination can provide and continue to trust in vaccines as one of the most effective tools to prevent diseases. Put simply, vaccines provide strong health benefits at a relatively low cost to society.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At a time when press freedom is under pressure and international newsrooms are shrinking, the Werner Holzer Prize celebrates a profession that many consider indispensable to democracy: foreign correspondence.

Presented in honor of Werner Holzer, the veteran reporter and former editor-in-chief of the German daily newspaper Frankfurter Rundschau, this year's award coincided with what would have been his 100th birthday. Holzer spent decades reporting from some of the world's most vital hot spots and championing international journalism.

At the award ceremony in Frankfurt's Römer, the city's historic town hall, Mayor Mike Josef recalled that fundamental rights such as freedom of speech and freedom of the press were first enshrined for all Germans by the Frankfurt Parliament in the nearby Paulskirche in 1848.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The 2026 winners reflect the breadth and ambition of the award. First prize went to Katja Gloger, a veteran Russia correspondent who moved to Moscow in 1989 and accompanied Vladimir Putin during the early years of his presidency.

In her recent nonfiction book, "The Failure: An Investigative Report of Germany's Russia Policy," Gloger and co-author Georg Mascolo offer a searing critique of the misjudgments and illusions that shaped German policy toward Russia for decades.

Industry observers note that second prize was awarded to DW journalist and presenter Jaafar Abdul Karim. His talk show JaafarTalk reaches millions of viewers across the Arab world and in Germany. Whether in Tunis, Beirut or Cairo, Abdul Karim tackles subjects that are often considered taboo.

A research grant went to freelance journalist Luise Land, whose current project explores why her German-Namibian family still owns extensive landholdings in Namibia today. By tracing that history, she examines the enduring legacy of the genocide against the Herero and Nama peoples by German colonial forces in the early 20th century.

In a recent development, "Katja Gloger is one of the leading foreign policy reporters. For decades, she has been among the foremost experts on Russia and speaks out on uncomfortable truths," the jury stated on Friday, explaining its decision to honor Gloger. "Like almost no one else, she has gained access to the very heart of the Kremlin's power elite — from Mikhail Gorbachev to Vladimir Putin.".

Recent findings suggest that at the prize-giving ceremony, Gloger delivered a passionate plea for more journalism — and more international coverage — in the German press. "We must defend trustworthy, reliable and fact-based journalism with everything in our power," she stated.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In a recent development, gloger worked for Reporters Without Borders for 12 years. "The latest rankings show that only one in 100 people can get their information from free, independent journalism and a free, independent press. That shows what's at stake," she remarked.

The prize winner also remarked she would dedicate the award to journalists in exile and to her colleagues at Novaya Gazeta, the independent Russian newspaper long known for its critical reporting on the Kremlin. Earlier this week, the paper was forced to shut down its operations in Russia and leave its Moscow newsroom.

Recent findings suggest that in his acceptance speech, Jaafar Abdul Karim stated journalism has become more challenging and exhausting than ever. The DW host spoke of hatred and incitement, attacks and threats, both online and offline, in the regions he reports on as well as in Germany.

Such pressure, he remarked, takes a personal toll — yet giving up is not an option. "When I listen to my heart, I know I have to keep going," he said. The answer, he argued, is a form of journalism that fosters dialogue, embraces multiple perspectives and helps bridge divides rather than deepen them.

Sources indicate that "I firmly believe in the power of dialogue, today more than ever. That's why we must talk to one another. Even when it gets difficult. Even when we disagree. Or perhaps precisely because of that," he said.

According to recent reports, listening doesn't mean agreeing, and understanding doesn't mean being in agreement. "Especially now, in times of polarization, when those who believe they're always right are often the loudest, we as journalists have a special responsibility. When everyone is just shouting into their own bubbles or communities, we need journalists who connect these bubbles with one another," he remarked.

It has been revealed that the jury praised Abdul Karim for creating programs at DW that reach millions of young people across the Arab world and in Germany. "His journalism fosters dialogue between countries, between generations, and between religions. He has set newly introduced standards," the jury stated.

So far in 2026, JaafarTalk has already garnered more than 1.1 billion views across all platforms, and its community has grown to more than 9 million followers. Its motto: "Diversity fosters dialogue.".

Sources indicate that "We need fact-based journalism that promotes dialogue and reflects the diversity of our society," Abdul Karim stressed. "By that, I mean an honest and open dialogue in which we do not look away or remain silent. On the contrary, we must take a clear stand against racism, antisemitism, Islamophobia, discrimination, sexism, and hate speech — no matter which side they come from.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Cincinnati Zoo has suffered an enormously devastating loss.

Fiona the Hippo—who first gained fame in 2017 after being born six weeks premature—has died after accidentally eating a visitor’s hat earlier this month, the Cincinnati Zoo confirmed.

It has been revealed that “We are in shock at the moment,” the zoo’s director Dave Jenike noted in a Nov. 19 press release. “We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn’t anymore.”.

According to the zoo, the veterinary staff tried everything they could to save the 9-year-old hippo as they attempted to move the knit hat out of her system.

“Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn’t fight anymore,” Jenike added. “She was dearly loved by her Zoo family and countless others around the world. Her loss will be felt deeply by so many.”.

The Ohio zoo asked the public to “keep the people who worked with Fiona and tried to save her in your thoughts and prayers.”.

In a recent development, the Nile hippopotamus’ health woes began on Nov. 8 when she accidentally swallowed a hat that a zoo visitor had thrown in the air, which a ceiling fan then moved into her enclosure, zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley had confirmed to the Associated Press.

Prior to her passing, the Cincinnati Zoo had been hopeful about her odds, saying in a Nov. 17 Facebook post that they were “monitoring her around the clock” and were “cautiously optimistic that she will pass it and return to her usual self.”.

Fiona—who would have turned 10 in January—also received a colonoscopy, courtesy of the Columbus Zoo, as well as an ultrasound, which showed that her intestines were bunching, proving that she was working on passing something through her body.

According to recent reports, much like her death, Fiona’s birth was difficult, as she was born six weeks premature in 2017, weighing in at just 25 pounds, the lowest recorded birth weight for her species ever. She rapidly became a celebrity across the internet as zoo staffers shared her progress with the world and less than two months later reached 90 pounds.

In a recent development, “Fiona was such a gift,” Cincinnati Zoo Executive Chair of the Board Thane Maynard shared Nov. 19. “I have never known an animal so beloved in all my life. From the day she was born, she was like lightning in a bottle. And, she will be remembered and beloved many years from now.”.

For a look back at Fiona’s larger than life moments, keep reading.

In a recent development, the zoo's 17-year-old hippo named Bibi gave birth to little Fiona six weeks early on January 24, 2017. She weighed 25 lbs. less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species, prompting critical care from vet staff.

It has been revealed that fiona's health made steady improvements in the weeks after her arrival, and by mid-March she had reached the 90 lb. mark, was eating hay and enjoying time in the pool!

Ever so curious about her surroundings, Fiona couldn't help but get an up-close look at herself on a computer screen.

By May, Fiona was well into the 200 lb. range and spending plenty of time lounging in her kiddie pool. What. A. Life.

Thanks to Fiona's tireless spirit and determination, she graduated to deeper-level pools after learning how to propel herself through the water.

It wasn't until early June that little Fiona began spending time with her mama. In the beginning, Bifi (as they were so lovingly dubbed) interacted during brief, supervised play dates but have since begun adjusting to life in the outdoor pool enclosure.

Fiona's dad Henry was reunited with his daughter one month later and from the looks of those hippo grins, their first time interacting went swell!

Fiona embraces all her curves and all her edges, and it's a much-needed reminder that we all should too.

It took much longer than anticipated, but Henry, Bibi and Fiona are finally cohabitating as a happy and healthy bloat. She can't get enough time exploring her dads' mouth, which is apparently normal behavior for a growing baby hippo!

In a recent development, without a finalized schedule in place, Cincinnati Zoo visitors should cross their fingers in anticipation of seeing Fiona out and about. Here she is laying a wet one on her caregiver. Mwah!

This mother-daughter pair spends their afternoons splashing in the pool like any hippos should. And aren't those faces priceless?
